OpenTable Regulars is free to join, and you'll earn 100 dining points for each reservation you book directly on OpenTable while signed in to your account and then complete. Reservations made through restaurant websites or third-party booking partners generally don't qualify. Points are posted only after you've dined, so canceled reservations and no-shows earn nothing.

Some restaurants in the program also offer bonus-point reservations worth 500, 750 or even 1,000 points at certain times. To find them, turn on the "bonus points filter" under special features in the OpenTable app.

Once you have at least 1,000 points, you can redeem them in the app's "Rewards" section at the following rates for U.S. members:

As for the redemption rate you'll get for each, they're:

That means a standard 100-point reservation is only worth 80 cents toward a future meal, and you'll need 20 of them to earn a $16 dining credit, which isn't very rewarding.

Dining credits work at participating OpenTable restaurants (look for the "Dining Credit Accepted" filter). After you redeem your points, you can add the credit to a reservation, which provides a digital Mastercard you can use toward eligible bills. Experience credits work similarly but only apply to certain prepaid experiences, such as prix-fixe menus and cocktail classes. Dining credits expire 12 months after you redeem them.

If you complete six reservations on OpenTable within 12 months, you'll then unlock Gold status for a year. Gold members get priority notifications when tables open up, a three-month complimentary Uber One trial for eligible new or returning members who do not have an active subscription and access to "Gold Tables," which promises harder-to-book tables at more than 500 participating restaurants in over 50 U.S. cities.

OpenTable also partners with Chase, Uber and Visa. Uber One members can book Uber One Exclusive Tables, eligible Visa cardholders can access tables and special events through the Visa Dining Collection and select Chase cardholders get exclusive tables and statement credits (more on that below).

Make sure you're actually turning up for your bookings, though. OpenTable will close your Regulars account and cancel all your points if you record four no-shows within 12 months. Your points also expire after 12 months of inactivity or after 3 years from the date you earn them, whichever comes first.

Related: Earn even more rewards when dining out with OpenTable

DoorDash is best known for delivery, but reservations are now available in select cities across the U.S., Australia and Canada. Its current market page lists 17 U.S. cities, plus Melbourne and Sydney in Australia and Toronto and Vancouver in Canada.

Rather than earn points, you earn promotional DoorDash credits when you book and complete an eligible reservation in the DoorDash app or on its website. The amount is shown before you book and now varies by restaurant, reservation time and membership status. Current U.S. listings commonly advertise $5 in credits, while some times display $10 or $12. Not every reservation earns a credit.

Credits are posted after you've paid for your meal and can be used toward eligible future DoorDash delivery or pickup orders. They typically can't be used to pay for taxes, fees or tips, expire six months after they're issued unless the offer says otherwise, have no cash value and can't be used to buy gift cards or alcohol.

Since the reward is a fixed amount, you don't earn more rewards for a higher food bill. A $5 credit is a 5% return on a $100 dinner but about 1.7% on a $300 tasting menu. A $10 credit would deliver returns of 10% and about 3.3%, respectively. That makes DoorDash Reservations especially appealing for smaller restaurant bills if you already use DoorDash.

DashPass members can earn more on eligible reservations, plus access exclusive prime-time tables and discounts on Lyft Black rides. However, the elevated reservation reward is no longer a simple fixed $2 boost across every listing, so check the offer shown before booking rather than assuming your membership guarantees a particular amount.

Check the restaurant's cancellation policy when you book. Late cancellations and no-shows may incur fees set by the restaurant, and DoorDash says excessive no-shows can result in suspension of your access to reservations.

Outside its reservation cities, DoorDash's "Going Out" tab also lists in-store offers at certain restaurants, with DashPass members earning extra rewards for repeat visits in some locations.

Related: Your complete guide to Chase and DoorDash

What is unique about this program is that you don't need to book through Seated: You link an eligible credit or debit card, then tap to activate the restaurants where you want to earn a higher reward rate before paying with your linked card. Eligible rewards then post automatically, with no receipts to upload.

Activations last until the end of the calendar month, and you can activate up to 25 restaurants per month (plus any monthly specials). Seated's app also advertises 5% back at participating restaurants, even without an activation, provided you open the app at least once every 30 days. Higher reward rates generally require activation, so it's worth activating your favorites at the start of each month and checking the offer terms in the app.

Rewards vary by restaurant but can be up to a generous 35% back, with the rate shown on each restaurant's page before you choose to activate it. Rewards are calculated on your eligible food-and-beverage total before tax and tip, so a restaurant offering 10% back would earn you $10 in Seated rewards on a $100 meal. Since each diner earns on the share they pay with their own linked card, splitting the bill doesn't cost anyone their individual rewards.

Seated partners with more than 2,500 restaurants in certain U.S. markets. Availability varies by city and neighborhood, so check the app for participating locations and current rewards before dining, rather than relying on a fixed city list.

You can then redeem Seated rewards for gift cards in the app's store tab, with available brands to choose from including Airbnb, Amazon, Dunkin', Nordstrom, Sephora, Starbucks, Target and Uber. Because rewards can then be converted to eligible gift cards at face value, TPG values them at $1 per $1 redeemed, provided you choose a brand you'd spend with anyway and meet any minimum redemption requirement.

The catch is that Seated rewards may expire after more than 30 days without qualifying account activity, so check the app's activity and expiration rules rather than assuming opening it alone preserves your balance. Seated also says its rewards can't be combined with other restaurant promotions, third-party deals (such as those available through Groupon) or discount offers.

If you're a new member, keep an eye out for a first-meal bonus offer of up to $10 through an eligible referral link or promotional offer, though this is not guaranteed for every member.

Related: Rove adds dining and in-store rewards in major platform expansion

Resy Rewards takes a different approach than the other three programs. It does not issue a stand-alone Resy currency. Instead, eligible U.S. American Express cardmembers earn 4 additional Membership Rewards points per dollar spent at participating restaurants, on top of the points their enrolled card already earns.

To participate, you must first enroll an eligible U.S. Amex card that earns Membership Rewards points in the Rewards tab of the Resy iOS app.

You must then book a participating restaurant through the Rewards tab, complete the meal and pay with the enrolled card. Merely dining at a participating restaurant or booking it through another part of Resy will not trigger the 4 bonus points per dollar. At launch, the program is only available through the Resy iOS app, meaning Android users cannot currently use it.

The initial New York City list includes restaurants like Carne Mare, Le Crocodile, Hearth, Kiko, Opto and Le Pavillon. American Express plans to expand Resy Rewards to additional U.S. cities and select Tock venues in 2027.

On a $100 eligible restaurant purchase, Resy Rewards would provide 400 bonus Membership Rewards points. Based on our valuation of 2 cents per Membership Rewards point, that is an estimated $8 in value (or an 8% return) before accounting for the card's standard earning rate.

Related: Don't overlook Resy: How to maximize dining experiences and save money with this Amex benefit

Because OpenTable and DoorDash reward reservations with a fixed amount while Seated pays a percentage of your bill and Resy pays a fixed number of points per dollar spent, the best option depends on how much you spend. Here's a comparison for $100 in food-and-drink purchases (before tax and tip), assuming the advertised offers apply and you can use the full value of the DoorDash credits on a later order:

If you spend $200 on a meal rather than $100, the OpenTable and DoorDash rewards stay the same, while the Seated rewards as a percentage of spending will quickly increase. Resy would also double to 800 bonus points, worth an estimated $16 with TPG's valuation of Amex points.

Seated can be the most rewarding option for larger restaurant bills, especially at restaurants that offer higher reward rates. However, its value depends on the percentage offered. DoorDash's fixed credits may still provide you with a better return on smaller bills or at restaurants that offer lower Seated rewards. Resy provides a consistent 8% estimated return from its bonus points — but only at its small number of participating restaurants at launch.

Related: The dining statement credits that save me over $1,000 every year

Certain restaurant purchases can also earn credit card rewards in addition to the benefits provided by these platforms. Combining these apps with a card that earns bonus points at restaurants can be an easy way to double-dip and earn more rewards. Some of the best options currently available include:

But it gets even better. Savvy diners keen on maximizing their rewards may be able to triple-dip by booking an eligible Sapphire Reserve Exclusive Tables restaurant through OpenTable and paying with their Sapphire Reserve card. Doing so will allow you to earn OpenTable Regulars points plus 3 Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar spent on the eligible dining purchase, even if you later receive a statement credit. Qualifying purchases at participating restaurants can also trigger the separate Sapphire Reserve dining credit, worth up to $150 per half-year.

Related: How to double-, triple- or even quadruple-dip on dining rewards

Resy Rewards offers a strong, straightforward points return at participating restaurants. However, the program is launching at only a handful of New York City restaurants and is available through the Resy iOS app, so most diners will not be able to use it regularly yet.

Seated has the highest potential return for larger dining bills. A restaurant offering 15% back would earn you $30 in rewards redeemable for gift cards on a $200 dinner, while a 35% offer would earn $70. Know, though, that higher rates generally require monthly activation, and you'll need to keep your rewards account active.

DoorDash Reservations can still be the best option for smaller meals when the booking carries a strong credit. A $10 or $12 reward can beat percentage-based programs on a modest check. The catch is that rewards now vary by reservation, availability is limited to select cities and the credits are less useful if you rarely order through DoorDash.

OpenTable Regulars is the least rewarding of the four for most standard reservations, with a 100-point booking worth just 80 cents at the best U.S. redemption rate. Still, it is the most broadly available of the four in the markets where its Dining Points program operates and offers useful extras, including bonus-point tables, Gold Tables and a three-month Uber One trial for eligible Gold members. Select Chase cardholders can also receive statement credits at eligible restaurants.

There's no single best dining rewards platform for everyone, as the right choice depends on where you live, how much you spend and how often you dine out.

Resy offers a compelling points return at participating venues, but its limited launch footprint and lack of an Android app make it more of a promising option than an everyday solution right now.

Seated can deliver the biggest reward on an expensive meal, while DoorDash can be particularly rewarding on a smaller bill when the booking offers a decent credit.

As for OpenTable, it remains the most broadly available of the four in the markets where its Dining Points program operates. Its nationwide coverage, Gold perks and Chase partnership make it worth considering, especially when you travel.

Since all four cost nothing to join, you may as well sign up for them all so you are ready the next time you want to book a meal. Just remember to show up for reservations or cancel within the restaurant's deadline, as no-shows can cost you points, credits or even access.

That's some food for thought before your next night out.

#6012. What Are The World’s Tallest & Highest Hotels? The Answer Is Tricky…

There’s something I really love about staying in a hotel room on a really high floor, where you’re so high up that you almost feel like you’re in an airplane. So, what are the tallest and highest hotels in the world? I want to talk about that in this post, and also discuss why the answer isn’t that straightforward.

The question of which hotel is the tallest and highest isn’t as straightforward as you might assume. And even once we do define it, there’s the question of the extent to which the answer is actually useful. First let’s cover the distinction between the tallest hotel and the highest hotel.

Generally speaking, the tallest hotel would be defined as the tallest building where a large percent of the structure is made up of the hotel. Most commonly, I see people suggest that this would include situations where at least 80% of the building is the hotel.

This is different than the highest hotel, which would be the hotel that is highest above the ground, even if it only takes up a small percentage of a mixed-use building, where there might be apartments, residences, etc.

In other words, a 50-story building that consists exclusively of a hotel would fall into the former category, while a 110-story building where the top 10 floors are a hotel would fall into the latter category.

With that out of the way, let’s talk about the properties that are remarkable in these categories…

First, let’s cover some of the world’s tallest hotels. We’ll define this as hotels where at least 80% of the building consists of the hotel facility.

Let me of course mention one downside of very tall standalone hotels — you could end up being on a very low floor. After all, if a high-rise consists exclusively (or almost exclusively) of hotel facilities, some people will end up on very low floors. The other downside, of course, is that these hotels are necessarily huge. If you prefer boutique hotels, you won’t find any on this list.

Currently, the tallest hotel in the world is Ciel Tower Dubai. The 1,042-room hotel opened in 2024, rises to a height of 1,227 feet (374 meters), and has 82 floors.

To go over the list of the top five tallest hotels in the world:

As you can see, it’s interesting (but perhaps not surprising) that all four of the world’s tallest hotels are in Dubai.

The Conrad Shanghai, meanwhile, is located in the Shimao International Plaza, and this is the perfect example of how it’s tough to define what is technically the tallest. While the building it’s in rises to such a high height, roughly 25% of that height is the spire. So technically it’s a very tall building, but the usable space isn’t as high as you’d assume.

If you ask me, the world’s highest hotels are much more interesting than the world’s tallest hotels. That’s because the world’s highest hotels typically take up the top floors of some gravity-defying skyscrapers, and therefore, they can also be boutique properties.

When defining the world’s tallest hotels, there are some general challenges:

Because of the above, there are some minor disagreements as to which hotel wins the title, but I’ll share my take (while acknowledging that I don’t have the ability to scale buildings with a measuring tape).

Currently, the highest hotel is the Rosewood Guangzhou. The 251-room hotel opened in 2019, and it’s located at the top of the CTF Finance Centre Guangzhou, which reaches a height of 1,739 feet (530 meters).

To go over the list of the top five highest hotels in the world:

As you can see, those last two properties are kind of hard to judge, and particularly J Hotel Shanghai is tricky, given that the property is split between different parts of the building.

As the inverse of the above, I should mention that the Armani Hotel Dubai is located within the Burj Khalifa, which is the world’s tallest building. However, it’s located at the very bottom of the building, so that’s hardly that useful, for these purposes, since the hotel only goes as high as 39 floors.

Lastly, in the interest of being thorough, if we’re going to define a hotel as being “highest” based on the altitude above sea level, then we’d of course end up with a completely different list. Hotel Tayka del Desierto is located near the Salar de Uyuni salt flats in Bolivia. It’s at an altitude of 14,800 feet (4,500 meters), so it’s generally considered to be the highest up hotel in the world.

I suppose depending on how we want to define “hotel,” there would probably be some simple guest houses at Everest Base Camp that go even higher, but I don’t think that’s within the spirit of what I’m trying to cover here.

If you ask me, it’s always fun to stay in a hotel room that’s really high up. There’s an important distinction between the tallest hotels and the highest hotels, though sometimes, the exact rankings are a bit blurred.

While I’ve long been interested in this, I enjoyed researching this a bit more closely, and actually having a (sort of) definitive list. Ciel Tower Dubai is the world’s tallest hotel, while the Rosewood Guangzhou is the world’s highest hotel (unless you want to consider the 120th floor of the J Hotel Shanghai separately from the rest of the property).

Have you stayed at any of the world’s tallest or highest hotels? Does it even hold any appeal to you?

i have stayed at the gevora in dubai once and really can't recommend it. i think it's an old apartment building that was converted into a hotel and needs refurbishment. also, you gonna spend a lot of time in the elevators / waiting for them.

@jmd001 same here, the view matters more than the floor number. Park Hyatt KL is a good example, way up in Merdeka 118 with the whole skyline and the Petronas Towers in the distance. FWIW free tools like Arbitrica or similar check the same hotel from dozens of countries to find kind of the lowest price in the world, since inventory and rates differ by country. Then ask for a high floor facing the city when you book

Having to take multiple elevators to get to the room is just not appealing to me. I”m happier in regular height hotel.

I used to request high floors specifically, but funnily over the years, it's something I don't really care about too much anymore. The main advantage of high floors in big cities to me is that it's quieter, with less road noise. However, I generally dislike sky lobbies, especially if I have to take multiple elevators to get to my room. In some cities, it can be nice for the views, but often it's more of an inconvenience to me. Plus, it just feels more personal and (yes) "grounded" to be in a lowrise that's not part of some megacomplex. It's something I've come to appreciate more over the years.

I only care about height in the context of what kind of view it gives me. So, first I would care about far AGL (Above GROUND level, not sea level) the highest room is (assuming I can get a room on that top floor). Then I would care about how tall the surrounding buildings are and how much they block my view.

#6011. The World's 6 Largest Airbus A321neo Operators In 2026

The single-aisle market has experienced a profound change over the past decade, with extended-range narrowbody aircraft replacing widebodies on transcontinental and regional trunk routes. At the vanguard of this revolution is the ever-popular Airbus A321neo, an airframe that combines unmatched fuel efficiency with transoceanic legs reaching up to 4,000 nautical miles (7,408 kilometers).

At almost any major airport in the world, the A321neo can be found, and that is for good reason. Across the globe, mega-carriers and ultra-low-cost airlines alike have restructured their operational strategies around this versatile jet, but which airlines have built the largest fleets of this aircraft?

This list will showcase the world's six largest operators of the A321neo, focusing on how distinct commercial models use the jet to redefine modern passenger aviation. These range from European ultra-low-cost expansion to Asian mega-growth and American domestic hub dominance.

United Airlines has emerged as a powerhouse operator of the A321neo, expanding its fleet to 80 active aircraft, per Planespotters.net, while maintaining a substantial order book of over 135 additional frames. As part of its aggressive United Next fleet modernization strategy, the carrier has leaned heavily on the A321neo to increase capacity availability on high-density domestic trunk routes and gradually replace aging narrowbody types.

Operating primarily out of its major hubs at Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD), Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), and Denver International Airport (DEN), the type connects high-traffic business and leisure markets that are vital to United's overall network. Passenger experience on United's A321neo fleet centers around a modern three-class cabin layout seating 200 passengers.

The aircraft features 20 domestic first-class recliners at the front, alongside spacious economy seating equipped with the carrier's latest NEXT interior standards. Travelers benefit from high-resolution seatback entertainment touchscreens, Bluetooth audio connectivity for wireless headphones, and significantly larger overhead bins designed to accommodate standard roller bags on their side.

The A321neo is incredibly important for United and its future roadmap. The aircraft provides the range and payload flexibility required to service demanding transcontinental corridors between the East and West coasts. Now operating these modern narrowbodies alongside incoming A321XLRs, United has successfully optimized its single-aisle network to match the capacity and comfort expectations of modern frequent flyers.

A uniquely liveried Coastliner featuring 20 lie-flat Polaris suites and massive seatback screens readies for transcontinental service.

With a growing presence among global leaders, American Airlines operates 96 standard A321neo aircraft, backed by a robust backlog of 127 additional jets on order alongside its separate A321XLR fleet. As highlighted in recent fleet coverage by Simple Flying, these narrowbody aircraft serve as the leader for high-density domestic corridors.

They connect major hubs like Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW), Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT), and Miami International Airport (MIA). Cabin layout choices emphasize a dual-class commercial strategy tailored for domestic business and leisure travelers. American Airlines equips its standard A321neos with a 196-seat configuration.

This layout features 20 domestic first-class recliners at the front, alongside spacious main cabin extra options providing extra legroom of up to 34 inches (86 cm). Passengers benefit from modern amenities including high-speed Wi-Fi, seatback power ports, and personal device entertainment streaming, providing consistent comfort across medium-haul domestic sectors.

Strategically, the introduction of these advanced narrowbodies has allowed American Airlines to retire aging mainline types and therefore optimize seat capacity on high-demand transcontinental and Caribbean routes. The aircraft deliver significant fuel burn reductions compared to older legacy jets. This fleet integration positions the carrier to seamlessly link standard domestic operations with premium-heavy long-haul missions flown by its sister A321XLR fleet.

As the largest carrier in Asia by overall fleet volume, China Southern Airlines is the preeminent Chinese operator of the A321neo. China Southern has 100 active A321neo frames in service, forming an integral pillar of the airline's domestic and regional trunk infrastructure.

Operating mainly out of its mega-hubs at Guangzhou Baiyun International Airport (CAN) and Beijing Daxing International Airport (PKX), the airline deploys these efficient narrowbodies to connect high-density commercial centers across mainland China. It also ventures into key Southeast Asian markets such as Bangkok and Jakarta. China Southern's A321neo fleet cabins reflect a tailored approach to regional comfort.

On this front, it frequently uses a balanced three-class or high-density two-class layout. Standard configurations often seat approximately 195 passengers, incorporating a dedicated premium cabin section featuring four business class recliners, 24 economy comfort seats with expanded legroom, and 167 main cabin seats.

The thoughtful partitioning allows the carrier to capture high-yielding domestic business travelers as well as servicing high-volume leisure demand on trunk sectors. The integration of the A321neo has allowed China Southern to greatly improve route economics amidst intense domestic competition.

What makes the A321neo so invaluable for China Southern is its ability to seamlessly handle multi-hour domestic and regional legs spanning up to 3,500 nautical miles (6,482 kilometers), encompassing the entirety of the major population centers in China. Ultimately, China Southern has bolstered its major hub operations with versatile narrowbody capacity, producing the operational flexibility needed to manage China's sprawling aviation network.

The largest A321neo operator in North America is Delta Air Lines, which operates a robust fleet approaching 111 active aircraft supported by nearly 90 firm future orders. As a cornerstone of Delta's long-term narrowbody renewal program, the A321neo operates high-density domestic trunk routes.

It connects major hubs like Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport (MSP), and Boston Logan International Airport (BOS). Delta's A321neo fleet is notable for its innovative cabin configurations, including a premium-heavy subfleet layout tailored for high-yielding markets.

While standard layouts feature 20 first-class recliners, 60 Comfort+ extra-legroom seats, and 114 main cabin seats, newly updated configurations incorporate an expansive 44-seat Delta First cabin. This high-premium arrangement dedicates roughly 60% of the aircraft to premium seating, meeting robust corporate demand as well as satisfying exceptional passenger load factors across competitive domestic routes.

Passenger comfort across the fleet is enhanced by comprehensive modern amenities, including seatback entertainment screens, in-seat power outlets, and high-speed in-flight connectivity. Powered by Pratt & Whitney GTF engines, the aircraft combines industry-leading fuel efficiency with a quiet, spacious cabin environment. Delta has positioned its A321neo fleet as a benchmark for premium narrowbody operations in modern commercial aviation.

India's largest airline, IndiGo, comes in at a close second globally in A321neo operations, with fleet counts hovering around 181 aircraft in service. Operating in one of the world's fastest-growing aviation markets, the carrier has turned to the narrowbody's efficiency to connect high-density domestic city pairs across the Indian subcontinent.

Simultaneously, it has extended its international reach into the Middle East, Southeast Asia, and Central Asia. IndiGo's relentless domestic expansion has been in part due to its high aircraft utilization rates, often turning planes around in under 30 minutes at busy hubs. What truly distinguishes IndiGo's position in the global A321neo landscape is its monumental order book.

The airline has hundreds of additional A321neos and long-range A321XLRs slated for delivery over the coming decade, pushing its ultimate commitment toward more than 600 aircraft of the type. As such, IndiGo is widely projected to surpass Wizz Air as the world's absolute largest operator of the airframe, as noted by The Hindu.

The massive influx of narrowbody capacity is fundamental to the airline's long-term growth strategy, allowing it to up-gauge high-demand trunk routes and significantly lower operating costs per available seat-mile. To support its high-frequency regional network, IndiGo equips its A321neos in dense single-class configurations optimized for maximum passenger capacity and operational turnaround speed.

Topping the global leaderboards as the largest operator of the A321neo is Wizz Air, the Hungarian ultra-low-cost carrier that has staked its entire aggressive expansion strategy on the type. Wizz Air has 185 active A321neo frames in service across its operating subsidiaries, including Wizz Air Hungary, Wizz Air Malta, and Wizz Air UK.

It is supported by a colossal backlog designed to phase out older ceo variants. Operating from key bases across Central and Eastern Europe, the airline uses the aircraft's exceptional fuel economy to open many point-to-point leisure routes spanning across Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa.

Wizz Air configures its high-density A321neos in a single-class layout accommodating 239 passengers, per Seat Maps, which is designed to maximize seat-mile cost efficiency. The ultra-dense seating arrangement features a functional pitch of approximately 28 to 29 inches (71 to 74 cm) alongside 18-inch (46 cm) wide seats.

This enables the carrier to offer highly competitive fares while maintaining strong profitability on high-density sun and city-break corridors. Like many other ultra-low-cost airlines, Wizz Air has standardized its cockpit and cabin operations around the A321neo, and in doing so, has cemented its status as the premier European champion of Airbus narrowbody technology.

Furthermore, the carrier is actively modernizing its onboard product to enhance passenger comfort in a way that does not sacrifice unit economics. Wizz Air has introduced updated lightweight seating partnerships with manufacturer Geven, alongside modern LED ambient lighting and advanced cabin features across incoming deliveries.

#6010. American AAdvantage Business Program: How To Earn Bonus Loyalty Points & Miles

American Airlines offers a small business rewards program, known as the AAdvantage Business program. This is a great way to earn extra rewards for your travel on American, including qualifying for bonus Loyalty Points and miles.

Best of all, eligibility for the program is surprisingly simple, assuming you have the Citi® / AAdvantage Business™ World Elite Mastercard® (learn more). There’s often even a bonus for new AAdvantage Business members, making it even more rewarding.

In this post, I’d like to take a look at all of the details of the AAdvantage Business program, as many people find it to be quite complicated. Note that AAdvantage Business was launched in 2023, replacing the previous American Business Extra program, which no longer exists.

AAdvantage Business is the name of American Airlines’ business rewards program. This allows you to earn extra rewards in a business account, in addition to the rewards you can earn through your own AAdvantage account. Best of all, you have quite a bit of flexibility in terms of distributing the rewards. Let’s go over the details of how this works.

The AAdvantage Business program has a pretty straightforward rewards structure, as it rewards members with both Loyalty Points and AAdvantage miles. With the AAdvantage Business program, you earn the following rewards, which will post within 72 hours of an eligible flight:

Let me emphasize that business travelers only earn Loyalty Points through AAdvantage Business when the business is currently eligible to transfer miles, and that requires either having the Citi AAdvantage Business Card, or having at least five unique travelers who have credited flights to the AAdvantage Business account, totaling at least $5,000 in flight revenue, over the course of a year (the credit card method is obviously easier).

Just to clarify a few additional points about AAdvantage Business rewards:

These rewards are all in addition to the standard rewards that AAdvantage members receive:

Just to be crystal clear, an Executive Platinum member ordinarily earns 11 Loyalty Points per dollar spent on airfare, while if enrolled in the AAdvantage Business program, they’d earn 12 Loyalty Points per dollar spent. There’s no reason to leave those bonus rewards on the table!

In order to be eligible to participate in the AAdvantage Business program, you need to have a business in the United States or Canada with a Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN) or Business Number. Even small businesses are eligible for this program.

The exceptions are that travel agencies, consolidators, wholesalers, and other sellers of travel, aren’t eligible to participate in AAdvantage Business. On top of that, AAdvantage Business technically can’t be used for leisure travel.

You accrue rewards in the AAdvantage Business program without any minimums, and then you can transfer the rewards to individual members, so that they can then redeem them out of their own accounts. In order to transfer the miles in the AAdvantage Business account to an individual AAdvantage account, you need to meet one of two requirements:

The AAdvantage Business program creates a huge incentive to get the Citi AAdvantage Business Card. That’s because just having the card allows many people to unlock the value of the AAdvantage Business program — there’s no need to actually use the card for your spending, but just having it is all that’s needed to redeem AAdvantage Business program rewards with no minimum on the number of travelers or revenue.

There are several potentially useful perks to this card, and on top of that, the card is offering a great welcome bonus, which is the reason that I applied for the card (and got approved), as that’s a nice incentive, beyond the value of access to the AAdvantage Business program.

It’s worth understanding how closely this card is actually integrated into the AAdvantage Business program:

For American frequent flyers with a small business, this creates a strong incentive to get the card. The card has a reasonable annual fee that’s waived the first year, and just having the card will allow many people to earn a sizable number of bonus miles.

If you’re curious about how the AAdvantage Business program works in practice, let me share some screenshots, for those who are more visual. Once you have an AAdvantage Business account, you’ll automatically become the travel manager for the account, and that means you can invite others to join your account (these should be people who work for your company, but there’s no verification process, as far as I know).

I should also mention that you can designate others to be travel managers as well, so that they can also invite others, transfer miles to people, etc. Travel managers must also be AAdvantage members who are adults and are residents of the United States or Canada.

To go through the process of inviting others to join your account, you’ll want to click “Invite people,” and then once they accept your invitation, they’ll show up on your account.

If someone’s AAdvantage account is linked to an AAdvantage Business program account, you’ll see that when you go to make a booking on aa.com, you’ll be asked for your “Travel type,” and can select “Business” or “Personal.” If you select “Business,” you’ll see that the company name populates, and you can select the name of the traveler.

Note that AAdvantage Business bookings are limited to one passenger, so if you have multiple people traveling, you’ll need to book as separate reservations. Also, to state the obvious, AAdvantage award tickets don’t qualify.

While the Loyalty Points from flights will post directly to the AAdvantage account of the member, the redeemable miles will post to the AAdvantage Business program account (the same is true for miles earned on the Citi AAdvantage Business Card). If you want to redeem miles, the only option is to transfer them to individual members, as you can’t redeem the miles directly out of the AAdvantage Business account.

If you’re eligible to transfer those miles, you’ll see the mileage balance listed, plus a “Transfer miles” button. There’s also a dashboard that shows your eligible number of travelers and eligible spending. However, as you can see above, I’ve met the transfer conditions even though I haven’t met the required threshold, since I have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

The process of transferring miles is super easy. You’ll just enter how many miles you want to transfer, and who you want to transfer them to, and then they should post to the AAdvantage account instantly.

My general take on the AAdvantage Business program is as follows:

The program basically offers an incremental 1.5% return on your American spending, since you earn one extra AAdvantage mile per dollar spent, and based on my miles & points valuations, those are worth 1.5 cents each. On top of that, the program offers an incremental Loyalty Point per dollar spent — that will have no value to some, while it will have significant value to others, depending on the extent to which you’re pursuing status in the coming year.

It is interesting the extent to which American has basically given up on corporate travel. American’s priority is getting people to book direct and keeping distribution costs as low as possible. So this program is intended as the major incentive for most small businesses.

American Airlines offers the AAdvantage Business program. With this program, the business earns one AAdvantage mile per dollar spent on eligible airfare, while the individual traveler earns one Loyalty Point per dollar spent. In order to participate and be able to redeem miles, you need a business with at least five registered employees who have each taken at least one eligible flight, along with $5,000 in annual spending, or you need to have the Citi AAdvantage Business Card.

What do you make of the AAdvantage Business program?

#6009. Dozens Fall Ill On Two Condor Flights To Frankfurt, Triggering Mass Casualty Response

Dozens of passengers across two separate transatlantic Condor flights became ill, causing a mass casualty incident response at Frankfurt Airport (FRA), as reported by aeroTELEGRAPH. While this is still being investigated, there’s a theory as to what happened, given what all passengers had in common…

On Saturday, November 21, 2026, Condor operated two flights from La Romana, Dominican Republic (LRM), to Frankfurt, Germany (FRA). Both flights were operated by the Airbus A330-900neo, with as many as 620 passengers onboard.

Flight DE3705 took off at 8:03PM on Saturday and landed at 9:23AM on Sunday, while DE3845 took off at 9:14PM on Saturday and landed at 10:35AM on Sunday. The flights had one thing in common, which is that between them, dozens of passengers became ill.

The illnesses onboard were so bad that a “MANV 25” response was triggered at Frankfurt Airport. That’s a German emergency response alert for a mass casualty incident — “Massenanfall von Verletzten” (though fortunately there were no fatalities here).

Passengers onboard were screened by medical teams, and one person on each flight was taken to a local hospital, while others are being monitored.

It’s not uncommon to hear stories of multiple people becoming sick on flights. Sometimes it’s a fume event, sometimes it could be a case of food poisoning (though it doesn’t usually happen that fast), etc. So what’s going on here, that people on two separate Condor flights became ill?

Well, the passengers on these two flights had one thing in common — they all came off the AidaBella cruise ship in La Romana, and then these flights were sold as part of the cruise package.

So while this is still being investigated, a norovirus outbreak on the cruise ship is believed to be the likely culprit. I’ve gotta say, an airplane seems like a pretty unpleasant place to come down with a gastrointestinal illness, so I imagine the lavatory situation onboard probably wasn’t great.

Dozens of passengers on two separate Condor flights between the Dominican Republic and Germany around the same time became ill, triggering an emergency response at Frankfurt Airport, which included a couple of people being hospitalized.

While it remains to be seen what caused this, the belief is that it could be some sort of a norovirus outbreak, based on the symptoms, as well as the fact that the passengers had all come off the same cruise ship. I hope everyone makes a quick recovery.

What do you make of this Condor incident?

#6008. Southwest Airlines' New 6-Hour Alaska Route Is Flopping: Here's Why

Southwest Airlines has not flown to Alaska for long. The increasingly evolving hybrid operator's first service to the Last Frontier was on May 15, 2026. Two routes were available from the get-go, with flights from Las Vegas and Denver, both of which are major cities for Southwest.

Many routes take time to develop, while some perform worse than anticipated despite strong enough expectations. An airline will often be able to tell how well a new link will do within the first couple of days of tickets going on sale. Initial data for Southwest's two markets suggests that one, in particular, might not be doing particularly well.

It is important to note that data from the US Department of Transportation (DOT) is currently only available until the end of August 2026, although that was only half-a-month before the first season's flights from Las Vegas and Anchorage ended. As it does not consider the full season, it is not fully comprehensive and is, therefore, perhaps somewhat unfair, especially given Alaska is a brand-new state for the airline. Treat it for what it is: a simple snapshot of initial performance.

Covering 2,002 nautical miles (3,708 km) each way, Southwest ran daily between Las Vegas and Anchorage in the first season. The DOT shows that 26,097 round-trip passengers were transported between May and August. However, the load factor was only 68.7%. That was over ten percentage points lower than the carrier's average load at Las Vegas in the same period.

This is just one part of the pie. What about fares? Cirium's Route Grader Report is currently only available until June 2026, so data provides even less of a view. In the first month-and-a-half of life, this new route had an average fare that was 17% higher than the airline's overall network from Las Vegas, but the distance was virtually double the length.

When this imbalance is considered, the new route to Alaska had distance-adjusted total revenue per available seat mile of 9.23 US cents, which was by far Southwest's worst result from Sin City. More than just this, it was the airline's fourth-lowest result across its entire network.

Despite only limited initial data, the DOT indicates that just under a quarter of Southwest's traffic only flew between Las Vegas and Anchorage. They did not fly elsewhere. Despite the carrier's daily service and 'relatively' low fares, it only captured 11% of the local market. In contrast, Alaska Airlines had 79% of it.

Southwest was massively reliant on those who connected to another flight at Nevada's busiest airport. The overnight service from Anchorage, leaving just before midnight and arriving at about 6:00 AM, is designed for that transfer traffic. Despite this and Southwest's considerable network from Sin City, the early overall load was not good (68.7%).

The low result was perhaps influenced by launching two routes to Alaska simultaneously, both of which have a similar schedule and both of which focus on connectivity. Analysis shows that the top ten markets from Anchorage via Las Vegas were Dallas Love, Phoenix, Austin, San Antonio, Sacramento, Salt Lake City, San Diego, Orlando, Ontario, and Albuquerque.

The US will have 44% fewer flights next Thursday, leading to lots of temporary changes. Find out more inside!

In 2026, Southwest operated nonstop between May 15 and September 14, with 123 round-trip flights available. In 2027, the first departure of the season will now be on June 3, three weeks later. The final service of the year will be on September 13. In total, 103 movements will exist, down by 16% year-over-year.

What is more notable is that the equipment has changed, although it is possible that it'll change again. For now, at least, the 175-seat 737 MAX 8 has been replaced by the 137-seat 737-700, contributing to a 34% reduction in seats for sale. Perhaps the MAX 7 will take over. The downgauge means that 14,000+ seats have been removed. Clearly, Southwest is taking big action to achieve stronger fare, yield, and load factor performance next year.

As much as I love the holiday season, it's my least favorite time to travel. Flights and accommodations are expensive, airports are at their busiest and winter storms can upend even the best-laid plans.

A credit card can't help your family pack lighter or ensure your flight departs on time. But the right benefits can lessen the sting from some of travel's most predictable pain points.

Here are the cards that can make the biggest difference during a hectic holiday trip, organized by the problem they solve.

Few travel fees are more annoying than paying extra to bring your socks with you — especially now that roundtrip bag fees can feel higher than the cost of the clothes inside.

For a family checking multiple bags, this may be the most immediately valuable benefit on this list. A card with a relatively modest annual fee can pay for itself during holiday travel alone.

Many airline credit cards offer a free checked bag, so start with the airline you fly most.

Higher-fee airline cards often match or exceed the checked-bag benefits shown here.

Many of the same airline cards that waive bag fees also provide priority boarding benefits. On a packed holiday flight, I'll gladly get in line early if it keeps my carry-on out of the gate-check pile.

The $895 annual fee (see rates and fees) offers another way to lower the cost of bags or boarding. Its up to $200 annual airline incidental credit can reimburse eligible expenses such as checked bag and seat selection fees with one selected qualifying airline (enrollment required). This is a useful way for existing cardmembers to absorb a holiday expense.

The (see rates and fees) offers a broader alternative: Its $300 annual travel credit applies automatically to eligible travel purchases, including checked bag fees.

Related: Which airline credit cards offer the best priority boarding perks?

Ever spend more time in airport security than you do on the flight itself? TSA PreCheck, Global Entry and Clear+ earn their keep throughout November and December.

PreCheck provides expedited screening at eligible U.S. airports; Global Entry includes PreCheck and adds expedited processing when returning to the U.S. from abroad; and Clear+ uses biometric identity verification to speed up the document-check step of security (so some travelers use it alongside PreCheck).

And for travelers who frequently cross between the U.S. and Canada, Nexus can speed up passport control.

You don't necessarily need a premium card to get these application fees reimbursed. Options include:

I like this benefit because it works regardless of which airline you're flying and gives you something that's often in limited supply: time. Just apply well before your trip because Trusted Traveler applications take some time to process. You can't open a card on Monday and expect to breeze through security on Friday.

The information for the U.S. Bank Altitude Connect has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

A lounge won't make a delayed flight leave sooner, but a power outlet, snacks and a drink make the wait easier.

These lounge cards offer different benefits:

* Up to 10 visits per eligible Platinum Card, per year to the Delta Sky Club or to Grab and Go when traveling on a same-day Delta-operated flight

I've had all of these over the years, although lately my favorite card for lounge access is the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite. The card's Priority Pass membership still provides credits at participating airport restaurants, which can be helpful when traditional lounges are full or there's nowhere left to sit.

There's a broader lesson there, too: don't choose a card based solely on how many lounges its network advertises. Check whether your airports have participating locations, whether there are restrictions on when you can visit and if it costs extra to bring your travel companions.

The information for the Bank of America Premium Rewards Elite has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Related: Is the Amex Platinum worth the annual fee?

Some premium-card credits seem easy to overlook until you arrive at midnight with no energy to navigate public transportation and ride-hailing fares are surging.

Food-delivery credits are also surprisingly useful at the hotel. I recently had Uber Eats delivered to my hotel because taking a cranky kid to dinner wasn't my idea of a good time.

For Uber users, both the and stand out. The Gold offers up to $120 in Uber Cash annually (distributed as up to $10 each month), while the Platinum offers up to $200 in Uber Cash annually (up to $15 each month, plus an additional $20 in December) for U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders.

Uber Cash will only be deposited into one Uber account when you add the Amex Gold or Amex Platinum as a payment method and redeem with any Amex card.

Platinum cardmembers can also receive up to a $120 statement credit for an auto-renewing Uber One membership, Uber's paid membership program for ride and delivery savings (enrollment required).

The counters with up to $420 in DoorDash credits (a monthly $15 promo for any eligible order plus two $10 nonrestaurant promos, through Dec. 31, 2029).

Its complimentary DashPass membership (activate by Dec. 31, 2029) also unlocks Lyft Go at no additional cost, allowing you to earn Lyft credits on eligible rides. Separately, Sapphire Reserve cardholders receive up to $10 in monthly Lyft ride credits through Sep. 30, 2027. (You'll need to link your DoorDash and Lyft accounts and claim Lyft Go.)

These credits alone are not reasons to pay hundreds of dollars in annual fees. But they can be genuinely useful when you're otherwise staring down an expensive ride or going to bed hungry.

Hotel timing benefits are especially useful when checkout is at 11 a.m., your flight leaves after dinner and no one wants to tote an overstuffed diaper bag around for six hours while your toddler desperately needs a nap.

There are two ways a credit card can help: through a premium hotel-booking program or automatic hotel elite status.

Those looking for boutique hotel experiences can access The Edit by Chase Travel℠ with their . These bookings provide benefits like daily breakfast for two people and a $100 property credit. When available, early check-in, late checkout and room upgrades are also offered. Cardholders receive up to $500 annually in statement credits for eligible prepaid The Edit bookings (of at least two nights; split into two credits of up to $250 each).

Similarly, cardmembers can receive up to $300 in statement credits biannually (up to $600 per calendar year) on eligible prepaid bookings through Fine Hotels + Resorts, The Hotel Collection and Airbnb Luxe through American Express Travel®.

FHR bookings include guaranteed 4 p.m. checkout, daily breakfast for two and property or experience credits. Room upgrades and early check-in are also offered (subject to availability).

(THC and Airbnb Luxe bookings require a minimum stay of two consecutive nights. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, FHR bookings will also require at least two nights to qualify for the lodging statement credit.)

These programs can be valuable when a nicer property is already part of the plan or you have annual hotel credits to use. Just don't let a possible upgrade or a few extra hours rationalize a room that costs twice as much as the hotel across the street.

Many hotel credit cards offer complimentary elite status. For example, the $95-per-year (see rates and fees) includes Discoverist status, which comes with 2 p.m. late checkout (when available).

Top-tier Globalist status extends that to a 4 p.m. checkout. The Hyatt card can help you work toward it with five qualifying-night credits each year plus two additional credits for every $5,000 spent.

Related: World of Hyatt Credit Card review: My favorite mid-tier hotel card

Hotel breakfast is one of those expenses that seems harmless until you're buying it for several people for several mornings.

These cards can help lower breakfast costs:

cardmembers can enroll in Hilton Gold status and receive breakfast or food-and-beverage benefits rather than having to apply for a Hilton card separately.

Rental car status is rarely about an upgrade from a sedan to an SUV, especially during a sold-out holiday week. The most valuable benefit is simply getting into a car and leaving the airport while everyone else is still waiting at the counter.

Capital One Venture X cardholders can enroll in Hertz President's Circle status**, which offers benefits including skip-the-line privileges, a wider vehicle selection, potential upgrades and a free additional driver. Meanwhile, the $95 Venture Rewards offers lower-tier Hertz Five Star** status.

cardholders receive Avis Preferred Plus and National Executive status, and cardmembers can enroll in complimentary elite status with Avis, Hertz and National.

In every case, the key is to enroll. Sign up and confirm your status appears in your account before you leave home.

**Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (i.e., at hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program, and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

Related: How to stack Venture X earning and Hertz elite benefits

These perks are only useful if they are ready when you need them. Before your trip:

Related: 4 things you really need to do now in advance of holiday travel

For holiday travel, the best card isn't necessarily the one with the longest list of premium benefits; it's the one that solves the problem most likely to cost you money or patience. A family checking several bags may save more with a $95 airline card than an $895 premium card, while someone planning a dream trip may want every perk they can get.

Opening an expensive card solely to make one trip less miserable isn't the play here. But if you are already paying a premium annual fee, this is the time to use the benefits you've paid for all year.

#6005. Qatar Airways Airbus A321LRs With Flat Bed Business Class Launching Soon

In the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first Airbus A321LR, which will be the carrier’s first narrow body aircraft featuring latest generation interiors, including flat beds. The airline will be introducing a “mini-Qsuite” type product on these planes, and we’ve now learned exactly when this new premium narrow body jet will enter service.

Qatar Airways currently has a total of 50 factory fresh Airbus A321-family aircraft on order. This includes 10 A321LRs and 40 A321neos — both of those are latest generation aircraft, with the A321LR featuring additional range.

The expectation is that the first A321LR will be delivered in the coming weeks, before the end of 2026. The 10 A321LRs should join the fleet pretty quickly, and will then be followed by the A321neos. The A321LRs will be configured with 160 seats, including 16 business class seats and 144 economy class seats.

The A321LR has a maximum range of 4,000 nautical miles, so it can be used for many destinations in Europe, Africa, and Asia. Below is a map showing the rough range from Doha (though in reality it won’t be quite as far, accounting for winds, fuel reserves, etc.).

Now, for those paying close attention, I should acknowledge that Qatar Airways briefly flew six leased, all-economy A321neos, but those were just intended as a temporary solution, and are now flying for Sun PhuQuoc Airways, which is running an interesting operation.

Qatar Airways’ A321neo-family aircraft order goes back a long time, and involved a lot of drama. The order was first announced in 2011, then the airline reconfirmed and upsized it in 2017. However, then former Qatar Airways CEO Akbar Al Baker got into a fight with Airbus over A350 production quality, and refused to take delivery of any Airbus planes.

That turned into a massive court battle, which was eventually resolved. But in the process, Qatar Airways lost all of its Airbus delivery slots, which is why these planes are coming way later than initially expected.

Qatar Airways has been promising all along that it would introduce some sort of a next generation flat bed business class product on its Airbus A321LRs. As you’d expect, business class seats on narrow bodies sometimes differ from those on wide bodies, due to differing cabin constraints.

What can we expect onboard these Qatar Airways A321LRs in business class? Executive Traveller quotes Qatar Airways CEO Hamad Ali Al-Khater as saying that the new business class product will be based on the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform.

These planes will boast 16 business class seats, in a 1-1 configuration. This product offers reverse herringbone seats, and Qatar Airways plans to have doors at each seat as well, of course with its customized finishes.

The launch customer for the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform was Air France on its A350s. However, that’s the wide body version of the seat, which is modified from the narrow body version.

When it comes to the narrow body version of the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, ITA Airways was the launch customer, on its A321neos.

This is also the product that Etihad is installing on its A321LRs. ITA Airways and Etihad don’t have doors in business class, but Qatar Airways does plan to offer it. Etihad also markets the first row of the cabin as first class (and that has doors), but I wouldn’t expect Qatar Airways to do something similar.

This is about as good as narrow body business class seats get, as it’s generally preferred to the herringbone seats you’ll find on other carriers, like JetBlue A321LRs, American A321XLRs, etc.

Qatar Airways now seems pretty certain about the delivery of its upcoming Airbus A321LRs, as the airline has officially put the first routes on sale, as flagged by AeroRoutes:

When you pull up the above flights, you’ll now see the seat map for the A321LR, which confirms the 16-seat business class cabin.

In the coming weeks, Qatar Airways is expected to take delivery of its first of 10 Airbus A321LRs. This will be the first custom designed next generation narrow body that the airline takes delivery of. We knew the airline would offer flat bed seats on these planes, and now we have the details of that.

The airline has gone with the STELIA Aerospace OPERA platform, the same product you’ll find on similar planes of Etihad and ITA Airways. However, unlike those airlines, Qatar Airways will have doors in business class. The planes will enter service by very early 2027, flying from Doha to both Vienna and Zurich.

What do you make of Qatar Airways’ upcoming A321LRs, and the planned interiors?

#6003. American Blocking Domestic Saver Awards Close To Departure (Within Six Days)

In May 2026, we saw American introduce a major new restriction for award travel, which had the biggest implications for those redeeming on American through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club (in other words, anyone redeeming through a program other than American AAdvantage).

With this, American started to restrict its own saver level award availability close to departure. Initially, all domestic nonstop saver awards within six days of departure were pulled. In recent days, it looks like American has expanded this to all domestic connecting itineraries as well, so I’d like to cover those details (thanks to azbobcat for flagging this).

Historically, American has been by far the best of the “big three” US carriers when it comes to making award seats on its own flights available, especially on domestic and short haul international flights. American actually releases a good amount of saver award seats across cabins, and it’s one of the things that makes AAdvantage better than the competition.

However, in May 2026, we saw American introduce a major change to how it releases award space to partner frequent flyer programs. Long story short, American started blocking all nonstop, domestic saver award availability, for flights within six days (exactly 144 hours) of departure.

As soon as a flight gets to the point where it’s 144 hours until departure, you’ll see that the airline “turns off” its saver fare classes — I’m referring specifically to the “U” (saver business class award) and “T” (saver economy award) fare classes, which show up when searching on ExpertFlyer, for example.

Initially, this applied exclusively to nonstop, domestic award tickets, as connecting itineraries and all international itineraries (including short haul international ones) weren’t impacted by this. However, this seems to have now expanded to domestic connecting itineraries as well.

So any wholly domestic itinerary exclusively on American is no longer bookable at the saver level within six days of departure. International itineraries continue to be bookable within six days of departure, whether traveling nonstop or with a connection.

What would cause American to suddenly “shut off” saver awards for domestic routes within days of departure?

What’s interesting here is that the implications for AAdvantage members are limited. Yes, American has shut off awards in the saver fare classes, but that’s not to say that American isn’t making reasonably priced awards available within days of departure. American has long used some kind of dynamic award pricing concept for its own flights, regardless of whether or not there’s saver availability.

It’s just that any awards in the official saver fare buckets aren’t available, and therefore aren’t bookable with points belonging to partner programs.

So it sure seems to me that the intent here is to block award availability for those booking through partner programs, like Alaska Atmos Rewards or British Airways Club. It goes without saying that I absolutely hate this restriction, as someone who “funds” a vast majority of my domestic American travel using Atmos Rewards points. At the same time, I also have to say that I can’t blame American for this change, as the airline has just made it too easy.

I’ve been booking basically all my travel directly into American first class using Atmos Rewards points — I just set ExpertFlyer availability alerts for “U” class, it opens up a vast majority of the time, and then I book. It’s not surprising that American finally got a bit savvier.

American is now blocking all saver awards within exactly six days of departure for all domestic itineraries. This means within that timeframe, there’s no “U” or “T” availability, which corresponds to the saver business and economy award fare buckets, respectively. Initially this only applied to nonstop flights, while now it also applies to connecting itineraries.

For American AAdvantage members, the implications are limited, since American can still make reasonably priced awards available, just not formally in those fare buckets. The practical implications here are that partner programs just don’t have access to these award seats close to departure anymore.

What do you make of American’s six day rule on award tickets?

#6002. The Billion-Dollar Companies Behind Half Of The World's Commercial Aircraft

Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

While household names such as United Airlines and Lufthansa dominate the skies in terms of fleet count, there are many companies in existence that have similarly sized fleets that do not carry passengers or cargo, nor do they operate charter missions. These companies never sell a ticket, operate a route, or pursue significant branding campaigns.

Some of these firms control fleets worth tens of billions of dollars, and one owns more aircraft than many of the airlines the public recognizes. The airline industry is composed primarily of two main financial systems: ownership and lease.

Many companies such as Delta Air Lines are known for owning a high percentage of their fleet, notably their older Boeing 717 or Boeing 767 fleets. However, the majority of airlines lease a portion of their jets, as many aircraft with long order backlogs at the manufacturer itself can be hard to obtain. Leasing is a common way to bypass delivery delays.

Most people assume airlines buy the aircraft they fly. Increasingly, that is not the case. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), leasing now accounts for more than half of the world's commercial fleet, making aircraft leasing one of the most important yet least visible sectors in aviation.

Rather than purchasing aircraft outright, many airlines rent them under long-term agreements from specialized leasing companies. The scale of those firms is difficult to appreciate until their fleets are examined. AerCap, the world's largest aircraft lessor, reported owning 1,501 aircraft and managing another 148 at the end of 2025, with an additional 283 aircraft on order.

Those figures make AerCap a larger aircraft owner than many of the world's biggest airlines. Meanwhile, competitors such as SMBC Aviation Capital, Avolon, BOC Aviation, and Air Lease Corporation collectively control thousands more aircraft worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

However, ownership and operation are not the same thing. If airlines do not own many of the aircraft they fly, why would they willingly hand that responsibility to someone else? While there are many sides to the discussion, the answer relates to the complexities of operating an airplane to begin with, which is far more involved than car or boat ownership, for example.

A new Boeing 787-9 carries a list price exceeding $300 million, while even narrowbody aircraft represent investments worth tens of millions of dollars each. Purchasing hundreds of aircraft outright would require enormous amounts of capital that airlines often prefer to dedicate elsewhere. Dry leasing is the most common and most cost-effective way to accomplish this cost benefit.

Aircraft leasing allows airlines to expand fleets without making the full upfront purchase themselves. Instead, leasing firms acquire aircraft from manufacturers such as Boeing and Airbus and lease them to airlines over periods that frequently range from six to twelve years. Airlines gain access to modern aircraft while preserving cash and reducing financial risk.

Hundreds of owned and investor-serviced aircraft

Hundreds of owned aircraft and major order book

While having direct operating authority of 1,066 aircraft, United Airlines' fleet also includes a subsection of leased aircraft, according to the SEC. This figure comprises 958 owned and 108 leased, at the end of 2025. This number is significantly less than AerCap's total number of active leases, which, on paper, causes AerCap to resemble a major international airline.

Four leasing companies own thousands of the aircraft that airlines fly every day. Here is how large their fleets are and how they got there.

In practice, passengers rarely notice that a different company owns the aircraft they are flying on. Under a dry lease, the lessor provides the aircraft while the airline supplies its own pilots, maintenance program, insurance, and operating certificates. To passengers, the aircraft appears no different from any other jet in the airline's fleet.

One recent example comes from Avolon's reported October 2025 sale-and-leaseback agreement with TAAG Angola Airlines involving 787-9 aircraft. In that arrangement, the aircraft are operated by TAAG, but ownership remains with the leasing company. Similar transactions occur throughout the industry and frequently involve new aircraft deliveries from Boeing and Airbus. An aircraft may spend its entire operational life flying for airlines that never technically own it.

A wet lease is an entirely different form of leasing, provided by companies like Heston Airlines, Hi Fly, or Wamos Air. The aircraft is frequently in the livery of the lessor, although not always. Further, the in-flight service, cabin crew, and standards are all those of the lessor company. Wet leases generally have a higher cost than dry leases, and are generally shorter in term.

The influence of lessors extends far beyond simple ownership. Because companies such as AerCap, Avolon, and SMBC Aviation Capital place enormous aircraft orders, they have become some of Boeing's and Airbus' most important customers. Lessors routinely order aircraft years before identifying the airlines that will eventually operate them.

This purchasing power became especially significant during recent supply chain constraints. CAPA reports that aircraft shortages and production delays have strengthened lessors' market positions by increasing aircraft values and lease rates. Airlines seeking growth often cannot wait years for new direct deliveries, making leased aircraft one of the few available solutions.

The result is that lessors frequently influence what aircraft manufacturers build, how quickly airlines can expand, and even which carriers gain access to modern fleets. A major leasing company may place an order measured in hundreds of aircraft, a scale that rivals the purchasing power of many national airlines.

Orders placed by airlines themselves to manufacturers such as Boeing or Airbus are typically more noteworthy. They represent a larger upfront financial commitment and a known destination for production aircraft. Orders placed by lessors are less noteworthy, but still significant from an operational standpoint.

While the end user of the aircraft is not known when, for example, AerCap placed an order for 100 Airbus jets, such an order boosts the inventory of a lessor. This not only provides options for customers, but an entirely different, and at times, more accessible way of expanding a fleet.

Leasing an aircraft engine is expensive, especially in today's industry.

The growing importance of lessors is increasingly tied to aircraft scarcity. Airbus and Boeing continue to work through substantial backlogs measured in thousands of aircraft. For airlines needing capacity sooner rather than later, leasing companies often represent the fastest available path to fleet growth.

Leasing companies also offer smaller airlines and startup carriers alike a lower barrier to entry to operation than buying an aircraft outright from the producer. AerCap provides one of the clearest examples. The company website published an order book of 283 aircraft entering 2026 while simultaneously managing thousands of aviation assets, including engines and helicopters.

That position effectively allows it to act as a bridge between manufacturers producing aircraft and airlines seeking them. Manufacturers in the aviation industry have the greatest amount of market control for their product. However, some of that power can be relinquished when a customer also acts as a distributor. The relationship between the manufacturer and the lessor creates an unusual balance of power.

Manufacturers remain responsible for designing and producing aircraft, but the largest lessors have amassed order books so large that they have become some of Airbus' and Boeing's most important customers. Companies such as AerCap regularly place orders measured in the hundreds of aircraft, allowing them to negotiate from a position of strength while shaping fleet decisions across dozens of airlines simultaneously.

The future significance of aircraft lessors will likely depend on one simple metric: access to aircraft. Airlines can only grow as quickly as new aircraft become available, and both Airbus and Boeing continue to hold order backlogs extending years into the future. Major aircraft manufacturers, while experiencing high backlogs of orders and record customer interest, can lose control of the end use of their product when lessors place massive orders.

That reality places unusual attention on companies such as AerCap, Avolon, and SMBC Aviation Capital. Their order books, delivery positions, and financing capabilities may determine which airlines can launch new routes, replace aging fleets, or enter emerging markets first.

In an industry built around aircraft availability, the companies holding the keys to future deliveries may become as important as the carriers operating them. The next major test will come as manufacturers work through production constraints and thousands of aircraft currently sitting in order backlogs move toward delivery.

Whether airlines continue shifting toward leased fleets or return to greater ownership could depend on how effectively Boeing and Airbus satisfy demand over the remainder of the decade. For passengers, the aircraft parked at the gate will probably continue wearing airline colors. The more interesting question is whether the real power behind those fleets increasingly belongs to companies whose names never appear on the boarding pass.
