Delta Air Lines flight cancellations spilled into Monday after a tech outage snarled air traffic on Sunday. Combined with bad weather, it's made for a messy start to the Thanksgiving travel rush.

By 7:15 a.m. EST Monday, Delta had canceled at least 92 mainline flights for the day. That's about 2% of its planned schedule.

It came after the airline canceled or delayed thousands of flights on Sunday following a problem with a key system that automates weight and balance calculations.

The disruption led to mass delays at its Atlanta mega-hub — the world’s busiest airport — and cascaded to other airports around the country.

Delta said it had restored its automated system by late Sunday afternoon. But the disruptions continued to climb as the carrier worked to get operations fully back on track — and Mother Nature didn't help, either.

Delta's operations appeared to be improving on Monday, but travelers still had to deal with some residual disruptions from a messy Sunday at airports — especially on the East Coast.

Around 70% of the flight disruptions were due to the tech issues, the airline had said. The rest were tied to Sunday's weather problems, and air traffic control delays that resulted.

“We thank our customers for their patience and our people for their professionalism," Delta said in a statement to TPG.

Travelers had other problems to contend with as the Thanksgiving rush got underway, too.

Mother Nature also slowed air traffic at some major hubs.

Low cloud ceilings and poor visibility fueled flight delays and led to dozens of planes getting diverted.

New York’s LaGuardia Airport (LGA) was most heavily affected, with nearly 60% of all departing and arriving flights delayed Sunday, per FlightAware.

42 flights headed to LGA on Sunday were diverted to other airports, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.

Many of those flights landed instead in Philadelphia; Albany, N.Y.; Harrisburg, PA; and Syracuse, N.Y.

These disruptions come a week after one of the most chaotic weekends at airports in recent memory.

More than 18,000 flights were canceled last weekend after an outage on Nov. 13 to critical Federal Aviation Administration technology.

Last week, a brief technical outage at United Airlines also fueled a host of flight delays.

What to do if you’re affected: This week, the TPG team put our heads together to offer some of our top tips for navigating a travel meltdown. Here’s what to know.

If your flight is canceled or significantly delayed, you’re entitled to a refund under U.S. Department of Transportation policy — but only if you choose not to fly.

If you get stranded in Sunday’s travel mess, it pays to know what the reason was for the disruption.

If you get stuck because of Delta’s tech outage, the carrier may be willing to pay for any hotel, meal and ground transportation costs you incur — if it’s a major delay. See details at FlightRights.gov.

The carrier on Sunday acknowledged it was providing those accommodations to passengers "when necessary."

If you get stuck because of bad weather, it's less likely your airline will offer any sort of compensation. But keep your receipts: If you paid for your trip with a credit card that has travel insurance, you might be able to file a claim and seek reimbursement.

These latest travel woes also coincide, of course, with the start of the Thanksgiving travel rush — with airports expected to be very busy with holiday travelers over the next few days.

All eyes are on next Sunday — Nov. 29 — which could be the busiest day of the year to fly.

Last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the most crowded day ever at U.S. airports.

#5986. Why Ultra-Long-Haul Flights Are Easier On An Aircraft Than Short Hops

Services like Qatar Airways' flight from Doha to Auckland and Singapore Airlines' route from Singapore to New York are among the most challenging flights in the world. They push modern aircraft to their limits, testing their range, performance, and fuel burn like no other. There's been a noticeable increase in ultra-long-haul flights in recent years, driven by the arrival of new aircraft like the Airbus A350 and Boeing 787 Dreamliner, which are more capable and efficient than earlier widebodies.

However, while these flights push planes to their technical limits, they aren't particularly physically demanding on the aircraft. Longer flights are actually much less stressful on the airframe and the engines than operating multiple shorter services in a given day with few breaks in between. Naturally, multiple factors go into how stressed an aircraft is during a flight, and time between flights also matters.

The lifespan of large transport aircraft is really determined by two measurements: cycles and hours. The hours metric is as the word implies, while cycles measure the number of times an aircraft is pressurized and depressurized. This roughly corresponds to the number of flights the aircraft takes, although airliners do occasionally operate flights without fully pressurizing the cabin (these are almost always ferry flights flown when the aircraft has a pressurization issue).

Widebody aircraft operating long-haul and ultra-long-haul flights tend to rack up hours very quickly, while short-haul airliners rack up cycles quickly. However, while hours are one measure of an airframe's lifespan, the number of cycles/flights operated is a more important metric for determining how stressed the aircraft is overall. Operating multiple flights means the landing gear and brakes are used for multiple landings, while the fuel and hydraulic systems also wear with each flight.

In addition, each flight involves the engines being pushed to takeoff power and, typically, the reverse thrusters being activated upon landing (this doesn't occur with every landing, but it occurs onalmost every landing). This puts strain on the engines, whereas an aircraft operating a long-haul or ultra-long-haul flight only performs one takeoff and one landing. The number of hours an aircraft flies certainly stresses the airframe, but its cycles and the number of flights it takes physically stress the plane even more.

Hawaiian Airlines currently operates 19 717-200s. These planes are used exclusively to operate between the Hawaiian islands, which means that they routinely operate eight, nine, 10, or even 11 flights per day. Most of these flights last under 40 minutes, so they're not racking up hours as quickly as a typical widebody. However, despite the short length of these routes, the Hawaiian interisland operations are considered some of the most demanding in the world.

The aircraft's engines are routinely pushed to takeoff power, then reverse thrust is used on the runway, and then this process is repeated multiple times per day. The engines are constantly being used and rarely have time to cool down. The landing gear and brakes are used frequently, and short turnaround times mean the plane rarely rests. What's more, the environment exposes the aircraft to salt particles in the air, raising corrosion concerns and increasing stress on the airframe.

737 MAX 7, 737 MAX 8, 737 MAX 9, 737 MAX 10

One of Hawaiian's biggest challenges was determining how these aging planes would be replaced. The engines on newer types like the A321neo and 737 MAX would not take kindly to the constant stress, while their fuel efficiency would provide little benefit. Ultimately, Alaska Air Group (which now owns the Hawaiian brand) opted to use older 737-800s from Alaska's fleet to replace the 717s, presumably scheduling extra downtime due to the aircraft's size and to allow the planes to rest more.

The A350's reputation as a 'passenger favorite' masks a more complex truth for flight crews, whose rest experiences can vary widely.

Hour and cycle limits are mainly used for pressurized aircraft because of the stresses pressurization introduces on the airframe. While other components of the aircraft also get stressed, pressurization is one of the largest stress factors. Each time the aircraft is pressurized, the fuselage expands slightly as the high pressure air inside the cabin pushes the fuselage against the low-pressure air outside. Over time, this can fatigue the fuselage, potentially resulting in microscopic cracks.

Regularly scheduled maintenance inspections uncover any potential fatigue cracks before they become a safety issue, but the pressurization cycle nonetheless puts significant stress on the fuselage. The pressurization cycle and these stress forces were a major factor in two mid-flight breakups of the de Havilland Comet in the 1950s, the world's first jet airliner. While it was not the first pressurized aircraft, no other airliner flew so high, and the intense forces from pressurization cycles fatigued the fuselage far faster than anticipated.

Metallic fuselages are particularly susceptible to the stress forces caused by pressurization, while newer carbon-composite designs are much stronger. This has allowed manufacturers to lower cabin altitudes by using higher-pressure air, which would ordinarily require a much heavier metal fuselage due to the added strengthening needed. Meanwhile, some business jets have even lower cabin altitudes while flying higher than airliners, which is justifiable as weight and fuel burn are less of a concern in private aviation.

Aircraft are designed to serve for upwards of 30 or even 35 years, so aircraft engineers design them with a specific service life in mind that covers typical usage across multiple decades. Manufacturers perform fatigue analysis to establish safe limits and inspection intervals for the aircraft, while working with regulators to determine the aircraft's lifespan. This is designed around the plane's intended mission, with widebodies and narrowbodies having vastly different hours-to-cycles ratios.

In addition to the aircraft's overall lifespan, various components may have their own maintenance intervals, with engines in particular largely on their own schedules. Overall, aircraft designers set goals for the expected service life of the aircraft and its components, and then work diligently to achieve them. In addition, the original limits set for an aircraft are often increased by the manufacturer later in the type's service life, usually via an upgrade that can be retrofitted onto pre-existing examples.

The A320 was originally designed with a service limit of 60,000 flight hours or 48,000 cycles, whichever occurs first. Later on, Airbus was able to increase these limits to 120,000 hours or 60,000 cycles, whichever occurs first. The 767, meanwhile, is designed with a limit of 50,000 cycles, fewer than the A320, but more hours. In addition, some aircraft types are converted to freighters later in their lives, and these projects often come with post-conversion limits as well.

Is there a possibility that Boeing will make an extended-range version of the 787 Dreamliner?

An aircraft's age is often quoted in terms of years, but this doesn't have much of an impact on its actual remaining lifespan. While age can determine factors such as reliability and which parts need to be used, planes can easily operate for upwards of 40 years if they don't exceed their hour and cycle limits. Instead, however, planes are largely retired for economic reasons, as maintaining an old aircraft that has operated for decades is possible but rarely cheap.

As aircraft become older, they become less reliable, and maintenance costs tend to rise. In addition, airliners require multiple types of maintenance overhauls, including what are often dubbed 'D checks', where basically the entire aircraft is taken apart, which come at a huge cost. Older aircraft also burn more fuel than newer ones, which makes it much more expensive to operate aging planes. Oftentimes, airlines will retire their oldest planes right before their next major overhaul, and then they get sent for scrapping.

Because aircraft are retired for economic reasons, it's actually rare to see them near their service limitations. What's more, aging planes tend to be used less often towards the end of their lives due to their high operating costs, which further slows the pace at which the aircraft approaches its service limits. As such, some aircraft remain in service for upwards of 40 years with small cargo operators and in nations such as Iran, as well as older 737s and A320s that are nearly 40 years old, since they remain within their hour and cycle limits.

#5985. Park Hyatt Dubai Reopening In 2027, After Full Renovation: First Look At New Rooms

In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed, so that it could undergo a renovation. That was probably good timing, given the massively decreased demand we’ve seen for travel to the United Arab Emirates this year.

The hotel is expected to reopen in the spring of 2027, and the first pictures of the new room product have just been revealed, as flagged by rota. Let’s take a look at those details, but first, I’d like to briefly talk about why I have a soft spot for this property.

Dubai is a city that has endless hotels at all price points. I don’t have a single favorite hotel in the city, as it really depends on so many factors, from what you’re willing to pay, to the area you want to be in, to how big you want the property to be, to what you value most.

After all, the concept of hotels in Dubai is a bit different than in other cities, given that alcohol is primarily only served at restaurants in hotels. As a result, hotels are very much the social scenes, both for guests and non-guests.

Anyway, the 223-key Park Hyatt Dubai opened all the way back in 2005, and I can’t count how many times I’ve stayed there over the years, going back to just shortly after it initially opened. There’s a lot to like about the resort:

To me, it very much fits into the category of being an urban resort, in terms of being a destination, while having ideal proximity to things.

There are just some hotels where you have such fond memories for a variety of reasons, and for me, the Park Hyatt Dubai is definitely among them. In part, maybe it can’t help but remind me of the “good old days” of redeeming Alaska Mileage Plan miles for Emirates first class.

Remember being able to redeem 100,000 Alaska miles for Emirates first class from the US to basically anywhere in the world via Dubai, with a free stopover there, and no carrier imposed surcharges? And that says nothing of being able to fly from the US to London with a stopover in Mauritius, and layovers in Dubai twice on a one-way (IYKYK). 😉

In May 2026, the Park Hyatt Dubai closed for the main portion of its renovation. If you go to the hotel’s website, you’ll see the following restrictions:

Park Hyatt Dubai is currently closed as it embarks on a defining transformation – a moment of careful, considered renewal in pursuit of an experience that is more refined, more exceptional, and more authentically itself than ever before.

Behind the scenes, every space and every detail is being thoughtfully elevated – honouring the quality and commitment to luxury hospitality that have made this sanctuary on Dubai Creek so singular, while reimagining the perfect stay.

With an anticipated reopening date of Q1 2027, we look forward to sharing more updates as that moment approaches, and to welcoming you back to a truly reawakened Park Hyatt Dubai. Because true elegance never stands still. It evolves – and in evolving, it is perfected.

As it currently stands, the hotel is accepting reservations for stays as of April 1, 2027. Now, the hotel is accepting villa reservations as of January 1, 2027, but that’s separate from the main part of the hotel. We’ve known that everything about the hotel would change, but not many renderings had been shared up until now.

One thing is for sure — there’s no denying that the rooms were in desperate need of a renovation, given that they hadn’t undergone any meaningful updates since the hotel first opened.

The hotel has now updated its website to show pictures of the new room product, and you can find those renderings below. I’m conflicted here. On the one hand, this looks much more luxurious than the old setup. On the other hand, the design just looks incredibly generic, and like it could be anywhere. I wish we’d see a little more sense of place.

On the plus side, the hotel’s grounds and general bones otherwise have a decent sense of place, so I hope that’s at least maintained with the updates.

Leadership at the Park Hyatt Dubai had been vocal about how they hope to charge much higher rates after the renovation. I think it’s safe to say that’s all up in the air, based on how the situation in the Middle East evolves. As things currently stand, I see entry level rates in April that are $600+, while I see the lowest rates in summer at $350+.

I feel like that pricing is very much on the optimistic side, but again, there are lots of moving parts with the Middle East hotel situation.

The Park Hyatt Dubai closed in May 2026, and is currently undergoing a full renovation. In recent years we’ve seen a new beach club and new dining outlets added, but this should be by far the most meaningful update since the hotel opened over two decades ago.

The hotel is expected to fully reopen in April 2027, and the new rooms look like a huge improvement in terms of how luxurious they are. However, there’s definitely a sense of place missing, so I’m curious how the overall design evolves.

What do you make of the changes coming to the Park Hyatt Dubai?

#5984. FCC pick advanced by Senate Commerce after Democratic boycott

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, talks with reporters after the Senate luncheons in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

The fight over partisan balance on the Federal Communications Commission snarled a Senate markup Wednesday morning as Republicans advanced a controversial nomination despite a Democratic boycott in an attempt to deny a quorum.

Republicans on the Commerce Committee voted unanimously to advance the nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs, a senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, to be a member of the commission, alongside several transportation and communications bills.

The fate of the nominations and bills could ultimately be decided via a challenge on the Senate floor, according to a Democratic committee staffer, speaking on condition of anonymity.

In a statement Wednesday morning, committee Democrats, led by ranking member  Maria Cantwell of Washington, said they objected to Thumann Severs’ nomination without a Democratic “pair” nomination and referenced a letter they sent to Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, on Monday requesting the nomination be removed from the agenda.

“Commissioner Anna Gomez could be re-nominated with all swiftness, as we have called for numerous times,” the group wrote. “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.”

Thumann Severs, if confirmed, would give the FCC three Republican members and one Democrat, Gomez. The three Republicans could then constitute a quorum on the commission, allowing President Donald Trump to potentially fire Gomez. The commission generally has five members, three of the president’s party and two in the minority.

Cruz said at the markup that there is nothing in the law that requires moving nominees in pairs, and that committee Republicans would continue their work on what he called a nomination that followed a “typical process.”

“Democrats will control the Senate, unfortunately, in January,” Cruz said. “But today is November 18th. The American people elected each of us to fulfill our duties, including advice and consent, for our full terms.”

Related: Threats to broadcasters hang over FCC nominee hearing

The Democratic staffer told reporters that because the committee did not adopt rules at the beginning of the 119th Congress, it has been operating under rules from the 118th, which required the attendance of at least one member of the minority party to constitute a quorum for reporting bills or nominations.

“The remaining recourse is to basically go to the floor and . . . make an inquiry in terms of what took place today, and then there would have to be a formal ruling by the chair,” they said.

They added that in determining whether the committee had a quorum to advance the nomination, “It would depend on how they view our committee rules from the 118th that we practice under for the 119th versus what the Senate rules are.” The staffer said they have not yet spoken with committee Democrats or Democratic leadership about plans for such an inquiry.

Democrats also previously boycotted a committee markup in March over an aviation safety bill left off the committee’s agenda, after which action was deferred. The committee later came to agreement and rescheduled the markup.

In their letter Monday, Democrats quoted Cruz from a 2014 statement about the nomination of Loretta Lynch to be attorney general.

“As you wrote in 2014, controversial nominees ‘should not be confirmed in the lame duck session of Congress by senators who just lost their seats and are no longer accountable to the voters.’ We agree,” the letter said.

On Tuesday, Sen. Ben Ray Luján, D-N.M., wrote his own letter to Cruz calling for the removal of the nomination from the agenda based on grounds that Thumann Severs lied to the committee.

“While Ms. Thumann testified she did not work ‘on any media-related issues,’ documents obtained through Freedom of Information Act requests demonstrate that she worked on several media related issues, including on commitments that Skydance made to pave the way for FCC approval of its merger with Paramount,” Luján wrote.

Democrats have criticized the FCC and Carr for allowing media consolidation, including by Skydance. There has also been bipartisan criticism of Carr’s threats against broadcasters for speech he disagrees with.

Luján told reporters Wednesday prior to the markup that he expects, under Democratic control next year, Carr and potentially Thumann Severs would be called to testify.

“I have questions. I certainly hope that Brendan Carr will voluntarily show up to this committee when invited, and that other rules and tools do not need to be used,” Luján said, responding to a question about possibly subpoenaing Carr. “But . . . everything should be on the table.”

Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., said at the markup that he spoke with Thumann Severs about her role at the FCC and her “lack of engagement” as the commission has made decisions regarding broadcasters. He also said he found her testimony at last week’s nomination hearing “comforting.”

“I have concerns with FCC action in regard to political speech, broadcasters, and she indicated in her answers . . . in a way that provided me with a level of comfort about her nomination in regard to that issue,” Moran said.

Moran also said he hopes to meet with Thumann Severs before her nomination is brought to the floor.

#5983. Aeromexico 787s Get Makeover With New Business Class, Premium Economy

Aeromexico is planning some major upgrades to its wide body fleet, which consists exclusively of Boeing 787s. This is interesting on many levels — we’ll see the larger Dreamliners get all-new business class cabins plus premium economy for the first time, we’ll see the smaller Dreamliners get the old business class cabins of the bigger Dreamliners, and we’ll see the airline adopt some Delta-style branding.

I first covered this several days ago, when this was quietly announced at an industry conference, as flagged by Seth Miller at PaxEx.Aero. However, the airline has now released a video on social media with additional details, so I’d like to publish an update to reflect that.

To start, let me provide the context that Aeromexico’s Boeing 787 fleet currently consists of 25 planes, including:

Aeromexico is planning on fully overhauling the premium cabins on these planes, as was announced by the company’s CEO at last week’s APEX FTE EXPO 2026.

The plan is for the 787-9s to get all-new cabins, and in the process, the 787-8s will get the old business class seats from the 787-9s. That means the 787-8s will get reverse herringbone seats, which are still competitive, but of course not cutting edge (though still a huge improvement over the pairs of seats currently on the planes).

The 787-9s will really become the next-generation flagship planes for the airline, though some patience will be required. The expectation is that the cabins will be updated between 2029 and 2031, so that’s between three and five years from now (and that assumes no additional delays).

We’ll talk more about the new business class product as such in a bit, but the idea is that the 787-9s will get business class suites, including a front row “business class plus” product. On top of that, the 787-9s will be getting a premium economy cabin for the first time.

The plane will also have 69% more premium seats than before. Currently, Aeromexico’s 787-9s have 36 business class seats, while the retrofitted planes will have a total of 61 premium seats, between business class and premium economy. So I suspect the business class cabin won’t actually get that much bigger, but instead, most of that premium addition will come in the form of the new premium economy cabin.

It’s also worth mentioning that Aeromexico is adopting some Delta-style branding, as Delta owns a 20% stake in Aeromexico, and the two airlines have a close partnership.

Aeromexico’s new premium products will be known as Premier One Suites Plus (the “business class plus” product), Premier One Suites (business class), and Premier (premium economy). It seems the 787-8 business class will just be branded as Premier One, given the lack of suites with doors. That all sure seems to be inspired by the Delta One branding that’s used by the carrier’s partner.

Aeromexico has published the below video about its all-new cabins, which gives you a sense of what we can expect.

A post shared by Aeroméxico (@aeromexico)

For those who don’t want to watch the video, below are some screen grabs.

Side note — is this new, or has Aeromexico been doing a cute tequila service for a long time?!? If I knew Aeromexico was serving shots, I would’ve prioritized the airline much higher on my list of products to review. 😉

While details are otherwise limited, we know that Aeromexico’s new Boeing 787-9 business class suite is from Recaro, as the airline is reportedly the launch customer for this new seat. However, the exact product hasn’t actually been named.

I believe this might be an evolution of the Recaro R7 product (LATAM’s newest 787 business class), which in and of itself was already an evolution of the Recaro CL6720 product (Iberia’s newest A350 business class).

It seems that what was unveiled earlier this year was the new Recaro R7 Horizon concept, which is the same idea, but with upgraded technology and customization.

Aeromexico is planning some big upgrades to its Dreamliners. The Boeing 787-9s will be getting all-new cabins, including new business class suites, plus a premium economy cabin for the first time. There will even be a premium business product in the first row, with the products marketed as Premier One Suites Plus, Premier One Suites, and Premier.

As this happens, the 787-8s will be getting the old reverse herringbone seats from the 787-9s, so that will be a meaningful upgrade as well. You can expect these new cabins to roll out between 2029 and 2031, so unfortunately patience will be required.

What do you make of Aeromexico’s Dreamliner plans?

#5982. New York JFK Terminal 6 Is Almost Open: Airlines & Lounges Moving In

New York Kennedy Airport (JFK) is currently undergoing a $19 billion modernization. While this includes all kinds of updates, the two biggest developments are the opening of two new terminals — we’re talking about Terminal 6 and Terminal One (not to be confused with Terminal 1).

As you’d expect, the opening of both terminals has been delayed, since airport construction rarely runs on time. Per the latest updates, the expectation is that Terminal 6 will open before the end of 2026, while Terminal One will open in the first quarter of 2027.

Along those lines, it’s looking like we might just be days away from the opening of Terminal 6, so I’d like to cover all the details we know.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open with a phased approach as of December 2026. To cover the very basics:

The below video of the terminal should give you a good sense of what to expect in terms of the passenger experience, so I’d recommend checking that out.

All things considered, this new terminal moving is awesome, given the quality of terminals at JFK otherwise. For those originating or terminating in New York, this should be ideal. For those connecting to or from JetBlue in Terminal 5, this will also make connections much easier. Meanwhile for a limited number of other passengers, this might make connections a bit more complicated, for cases where airlines are moving away from their partners (like Cathay Pacific moving from American’s Terminal 8 to Terminal 6).

Roughly 17 airlines are expected to eventually operate out of JFK Terminal 6, though that will happen in two phases. Broadly speaking, we’ll see some JetBlue operations move there (since the airline is a core tenant), and on top of that, we’ll largely see airlines move from Terminal 1, Terminal 7, and Terminal 8.

So the expectation is that the following airlines will eventually operate from JFK Terminal 6:

There is still a bit of a mystery as to the order in which airlines will move to JFK Terminal 6. For one, there’s the two phases of the terminal opening, but even within each phase, it won’t fully be overnight.

We know that All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Condor, Frontier, Lufthansa Group carriers, and TAP Air Portugal, will move in the first phase. Meanwhile we know that Air India will move in the second phase. But for the remainder of the airlines, there’s a lack of certainty on that front.

Now, we’ll see if this sticks, and how accurate it is, but current schedule filings suggest that Condor will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 3, while Cathay Pacific will start operating out of Terminal 6 as of December 15 (thanks to Peter_ for flagging this). So it sounds like we could potentially be just over a week from the first airline moving, which would be awesome!

In terms of lounges, we have confirmation that Terminal 6 will have outposts from Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, Aer Lingus, and Air India. Hopefully the new lounges are ready to go as airlines make the move, but I wouldn’t consider that to be a sure thing, given the complexity of airport operations.

The Air India lounge definitely won’t open anytime soon, since the airline is only moving in the second phase. Meanwhile the Cathay Pacific, Lufthansa, and Aer Lingus lounges, will hopefully open soon(ish). Of course I’m most excited to see what Cathay Pacific has in store, given its amazing lounge quality.

JFK Terminal 6 is expected to open before the end of 2026, and if current filings are to be believed, the move could happen as soon as early December. It appears that Condor and Cathay Pacific might be among the first airlines to move, so hopefully Cathay Pacific’s new lounge isn’t too far behind. So we’ll mark this as “developing,” but the completion of the first exciting phase of this $19 billion project is imminent.

Are you excited for the new JFK Terminal 6?

After shopping for everyone else over Black Friday and Cyber Monday, it's your turn on Travel Tuesday. As you plan something for yourself, Capital One wants to help you book it for less.

Beginning Dec. 1, Capital One will offer eligible cardholders limited-time savings on hotels, rental cars, flight-and-stay packages and premium vacation rentals through Capital One Travel.

Some of these deals are more useful than others. Here's who can use each one and how to tell whether the savings are worth booking now.

Capital One is highlighting five offers this year:

The Washington, D.C., hotel offer ends Dec. 7 or when supplies run out, whichever comes first. The Hertz offer runs through Dec. 15, while supplies last.

The other offers each carry their own booking window, travel dates and terms, which you'll find in your Travel Wallet once the deals go live.

Related reading: Capital One Travel: How to book flights, hotels and more

Travel Tuesday offers are available to eligible holders of the:

That's a wide group, but not every cardholder will see every promotion. Premium vacation rental discounts are targeted to select Venture and Venture X cardholders, and not all Capital One cardholders have access to Premier and Lifestyle Collection hotel stays.

To check your personal offers, log in to Capital One Travel starting Dec. 1.

Related reading: The best Capital One credit cards

This year's deals are a perfect example of "when it works, it really works."

Some offers can save hundreds, but only if they match a trip you already wanted to take.

The hotel discount could save you $150 off $500, for example. That's meaningful savings if Washington, D.C. or Florida are already in your travel plans. But if you're traveling anywhere else, that discount is irrelevant.

The complimentary fourth night sounds valuable, particularly if you were already considering one of Capital One's curated collections. But it's worth noting that Capital One Travel already offers the fourth night free at select Premier and Lifestyle Collection hotels — this isn't a new deal for Travel Tuesday.

Similarly, the vacation rental offer appears to be a version of a targeted offer already in my account. Without waiting for Travel Tuesday, I already have a $200 discount available toward premium rentals in my Venture X account. There's no indication that the upcoming deals will raise my offer, though Capital One advertises that some cardholders may be targeted for up to $500 off.

Additionally, Capital One's collection of vacation rentals skews toward higher-end properties. Even with a discount, budget travelers may do better searching a wider selection of properties on Airbnb or Vrbo.

Lastly, the 15% discount on qualifying Hertz rentals is great when Hertz is already competitively priced, but it might not be high enough to change your plans if another brand is offering a better deal. Keep in mind that the Venture card family includes Hertz elite status after enrollment: Eligible Venture X cardholders can enroll in President's Circle status*, while Venture and VentureOne cardholders can enroll in Five Star status*.

The flight-and-stay package discounts require more comparison shopping because Capital One hasn't shared a standard discount. You'll need to check the cost of booking the same flights and hotel separately.

*Upon enrollment, accessible through the Capital One website or mobile app, eligible cardholders will remain at that status level through the duration of the offer. Please note, enrolling through the normal Hertz Gold Plus Rewards enrollment process (e.g. at Hertz.com) will not automatically detect a cardholder as being eligible for the program and cardholders will not be automatically upgraded to the applicable status tier. Additional terms apply.

The Venture X is the biggest winner. Cardholders may have access to the widest range of promotions. The card earns 10 Capital One miles per dollar spent on hotels and rental cars plus 5 miles per dollar spent on flights and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel.

The free fourth night is a standing perk, and the vacation rental discounts may already be in your Travel Wallet. Use this as your opportunity to re-familiarize yourself to card benefits you may have available year-round.

The genuinely new deals are the hotel discounts in D.C. and Florida, the Hertz savings and the flight-and-stay packages. If any of these fit your plans, even one well-matched offer can make a difference in your travel budget.

#5979. Sanders: ‘Medicare for All’ will be HELP priority

Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., holds a news conference in the Capitol on Nov. 10. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Saying that “Medicare for All” is no longer “a radical idea,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he would prioritize passing the universal health care plan if he assumes the chairmanship of the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year as expected.

Democrats could bring it about through the filibuster-proof budget reconciliation process, the Vermont independent and avowed democratic socialist told reporters. And the idea could be buoyed by an influx of progressive lawmakers elected in the midterms.

Sanders said Medicare for All is gaining support from voters across the country who are looking to overhaul the American health care system as costs have soared. Democrats on the committee will move the legislation “as aggressively as we can, as rapidly as we can,” he said.

His version, introduced in April and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, would implement the universal health care system over four years. In the first year, the the age of Medicare eligibility would drop to 55 from 65, while coverage would expand to include dental, hearing and vision care. The bill would also provide coverage for eligible children during the first year.

The age of eligibility would fall another 10 years in each of the following years until the fourth year, when coverage would be extended to all Americans.

“If there has ever been a time in the modern history of our country . . . to address the crises facing working families, this is that time,” Sanders said, noting that Democrats will have a 56-44 majority when the 120th Congress begins in January, the largest margin for either party in 16 years.

Sen. Tammy Baldwin, D-Wis., along with nine other Senate Democrats, last week offered an alternative Medicare expansion plan, which would lower the eligibility to those ages 50 and up.

While who will be leading Senate Democrats is still an open question — Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is challenging Charles E. Schumer of New York, who has been the top Senate Democrat since 2017 — Sanders said he is confident the Medicare for All bill will get to the Senate floor, “no matter who the [Senate majority] leader is.” Sanders previously expressed opposition to Schumer leading the conference.

Asked about efforts to extend the Affordable Care Act enhanced subsidies, Sanders responded he’s “all in.” However, he added “the American people and elected officials understand the current health care system is broken.”

Subsidies that help enrollees pay for health care premiums on the ACA exchanges were expanded during the COVID-19 pandemic, but these enhanced credits expired at the end of last year, raising costs for many who relied on them to help defray costs.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, nominated on Wednesday to be speaker next year, previously outlined broader health care priorities such as extending the ACA tax credits and reversing Medicaid cuts enacted in Republicans' reconciliation package last year. When asked Tuesday how far Democrats want to lower the Medicare eligibility age, Jeffries responded, “that’s all part of an ongoing conversation.”

In addition to expanding Medicare coverage, Sanders reiterated his push to lower prescription drug prices. The Vermont lawmaker previously introduced legislation aimed at reducing the cost of brand name prescription drugs by linking domestic prices to international price benchmarks.

To enact some of the agenda, Sanders may have to court Republicans.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said last week that he plans to serve as the top Republican on the HELP committee next year. Sanders said Wednesday that his likely GOP counterpart “has shown an enormous amount of courage in taking on Republican leadership year after year.”

Sanders added that although Paul may have a different viewpoint from himself on committee issues, he looks forward to finding common ground.

#5978. Capital One Venture Card Bonus: 75K Miles + $300 Credit Welcome Offer (Last Chance)

At the moment, the $95 annual fee Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card is offering a phenomenal limited time welcome bonus, making it the ideal time to apply. I’d like to provide an update that this is the last chance to pick up the card with this offer, as it’s expected to be pulled soon.

Not only is this among the best offers we’ve seen on the card, but this is also a reasonably priced travel rewards card that offers long term value, especially for everyday spending.

Link: Learn more about the Capital One Venture Card

The Capital One Venture Card is currently offering a limited time, lucrative, two-part welcome offer, whereby you can earn 75,000 Capital One bonus miles, plus a $300 Capital One Travel stays credit, after spending $4,000 within the first three months.

For context, Capital One miles can be redeemed for a minimum of one cent each, meaning the 75,000 miles will get you at least $750 in value. However, I value the miles at 1.7 cents each based on my latest analysis (see my methodology here), thanks to the value you can get by transferring the miles to travel partners. That means that to me, the 75,000 miles are worth $1,275.

There are lots of great ways to redeem Capital One miles, as they can be transferred to Capital One’s roughly 20 airline and hotel partners. That’s my preferred use of them, as you can get some amazing travel experiences this way.

Partners include programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, Singapore Airlines KrisFlyer, Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, and more. These are all programs that allow you to really maximize your points and get outsized value. Just to give a couple of examples of Capital One mileage redemption opportunities:

That doesn’t include the value of the $300 Capital One Travel credit, which posts upon account approval (rather than upon completing minimum spending). The idea is that this can be used for a hotel or vacation rental booking through Capital One Travel in your first cardmember year (in the first 12 months), and it’s valid across one or multiple stays. In other words, you could use it to pay virtually nothing for a $300 hotel stay. All-in-all, I’d say the Capital One Venture bonus is worth up to $1,575.

By my valuation, the current Capital One Venture Card bonus is the best publicly available offer that we’ve seen in over five years, so that makes this the ideal time to apply, and I absolutely wouldn’t wait for a better offer. Quite to the contrary, when this limited time offer gets pulled, it’ll almost certainly be worse.

For context, below is a history of the publicly available bonuses that we’ve seen on the Capital One Venture in recent years.

As you can see, we’ve never seen a publicly available welcome offer of over 75,000 miles, in terms of the mileage component. We have in the past seen $250 travel credits offered along with the miles, and this time around the travel credit is bigger. So offers really don’t get better than this on the card.

When you look at the bonus terms on the Capital One Venture Card, you’ll find the following language:

You are not eligible for this product if you have received a new cardmember bonus for the Capital One Venture card or the Capital One Venture X card in the past 48 months.

As you can see, the card follows a 48-month rule, so you’re not eligible for the welcome bonus on this card if you’ve received a new cardmember bonus on this exact card or on the Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) in the past 48 months.

Other than that, eligibility is unrelated to having any other credit card, and Capital One doesn’t have many consistent restrictions when it comes to getting approved for cards.

The Capital One Venture Card has a reasonable $95 annual fee, and offers a variety of perks beyond the excellent welcome bonus:

While the Capital One Venture Card is awesome, how does it compare to the Capital One Venture X Card, which is Capital One’s ultra premium credit card? The Venture X has a $395 annual fee, so the fee is significantly higher, but it also offers several great perks that should more than justify the annual fee. Among other things, the Venture X offers:

So when it comes to the Capital One Venture vs. Venture X, personally I think the Venture X is an even better value than the Venture. However, I know some people just want to avoid higher annual fee cards in general, so for those people, the Venture could be a better option.

The limited time Capital One Venture Card bonus currently offers 75,000 Capital One miles plus a $300 Capital One Travel credit upon completing minimum spending. This Capital One Venture bonus is significantly better than usual, so if you’re eligible for the card based on the 48-month bonus rule, I’d absolutely recommend applying. This is the last chance, as the offer is expected to be pulled soon.

Anyone plan to pick up the Capital One Venture Card with this great bonus?

#5977. Grand Theft Auto VI and How We Spend Our Time

Your time on earth, no matter how long, is shorter than you think. Do you want to spend it doing chores in a simulated environment?

A gamer plays Grand Theft Auto VI during an unofficial launch party at OS Gaming Lounge in New York City on November 19, 2026.

Donald Trump just met with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China for a tripartite global summit — and nobody has any real news to report, except for Trump, so desperate for media attention that he’s giving interviews to anyone holding a hot mic and a video camera. The lack of news is not just because of a (predictable) blackout enforced by the Chinese Communist Party, but because the collective consciousness of America has shut down for the next few days. If you thought the traditional four-day Thanksgiving Day Weekend was typically slow, get ready for a one-and-a-half-week productivity dip in the economy as the video game Grand Theft Auto VI goes live across the nation. Even National Review, as sober-minded as it is, has more than a few fans of the series on its staff.

Every periodical you might care to read — even the political or news-based ones — has brought forward its big-think “review” of the game, now available on PlayStation and Xbox. For all I know we’ll be publishing one too. But I am not a gamer — not in the modern sense of the word, although I did whip out my copy of Battletoads for the NES the other day to prove that I’ve still “got it” — and this will not be a review of GTA VI. Instead, I want to talk about time spent — and time wasted.

A gamer plays Grand Theft Auto VI during an unofficial launch party at OS Gaming Lounge in New York City on November 19, 2026.

Jeffrey Blehar is a National Review staff writer living in Chicago. He is also the co-host of National Review’s Political Beats podcast, which explores the great music of the modern era with guests from the political world happy to find something non-political to talk about.

On “Grand Theft Auto VI and How We Spend Our Time”

#5976. Restored to Calder’s plan, the clouds are spinning again

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., speaks during a ceremony marking the restoration of Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture in the Hart Senate Office Building atrium on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The day after Alexander Calder presented his plan for a public art display in the Hart Building’s nine-story atrium to the Architect of the Capitol, he died.

Fifty years later, Alexander S.C. Rower felt a sense of awe as he stared up at his grandfather’s work, finally restored to what he had envisioned.

“It’s totally phenomenal,” he said, pointing up at the now-moving clouds as he spoke, spinning his finger around. “It’s not entertainment, but it’s trying to emulate naturalness, trying to emulate what nature would do.”

It was a long time coming for Rower, who remembers traveling to the Capitol in his 20s for the original dedication of the Mountains and Clouds sculpture in 1987. The mobile portion stopped rotating as Calder intended in the 1990s, and it was ultimately removed in 2014 after being deemed unsafe by the Architect of the Capitol. Millions of dollars in private philanthropy later, Calder’s clouds are spinning again.

Rower was back on the Hill on Wednesday for an event celebrating the restoration, joining Architect of the Capitol Thomas Austin, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Angus King, I-Maine, and James Lankford, R-Okla., and the project’s donors. As the speakers addressed the crowd, the clouds began to speed up slightly. Onlookers gathered on the balconies overlooking the atrium and peeked through office windows. Attendees left with tote bags emblazoned with images of Calder’s art.

According to Rower, who leads the Calder Foundation dedicated to preserving and interpreting his grandfather’s art, the mobile is rotating on a 15-hour cycle that is “totally variable.”

“It can go a little faster; it can go a little slower,” he said. “I told the team today that during lunchtime, I want it to speed up just a little bit because everyone’s going to lunch. There’ll be … a lot of activity passing through, and then right at 2:30, well, let’s make it go quieter.”

It was a labor of love for those involved, and not an inexpensive one. Jon and Kim Shirley funded the $12 million restoration. Because the pieces were so large, they were transported on an extra-wide load truck and driven at a speed of 35 miles per hour from Michigan.

“We had to call every senator or governor that we knew on that route, which went through seven states, to get permissions,” he said. “That was a huge thing to overcome, and it all happened over a weekend. So my wife was actually on the phone with a governor’s wife on Saturday evening. The next day, he called up his Department of Transportation and got a permit.”

Christian Quilici, who helped manage the project on behalf of the Shirleys and said he serves as a liaison between the foundation and Congress, said the hardest part of the project was the size of it.

“We had to tear the wall down on C Street, which nobody really thought of in the beginning,” he said. “Nobody got how big this was until it showed up on their doorstep.”

Quilici said he spent years educating at least 30 different senators about the quest to reunite the mobile with the stationary mountains left behind. Some of the biggest champions were seated in the front row at Wednesday’s event, including Senate Democratic Whip Richard J. Durbin. Absent was Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who has been away from the Capitol while recovering from a stroke but has been a supporter of the sculpture’s restoration for years, pressing former acting Architect of the Capitol Joseph DiPietro on it at a 2024 Senate Legislative Branch Appropriations budget hearing.

“Is there any chance that before I leave the Senate, or at least before I die, we can get the clouds back up there?” Murphy said at the time.

Padilla read a letter on Wednesday from Murphy, whose state was Calder’s home for much of his life.

“This statue is actually a statement on our democracy, that we have big pieces of monumental art right in the middle of our most important and most iconic government buildings. To get this piece of art restored to how it was designed by the artist, well, that’s good for Connecticut. But I also like to think … it’s good for democracy too,” Murphy’s statement said.

The restoration was funded entirely by donations from the Shirleys, who are prominent Calder collectors, according to Rower.

“It’s very emotional to see the work completed after 10 years of us working so hard with the Architect of the Capitol and Calder Foundation. It’s a very overpowering, overwhelming emotion,” said Kim Shirley.

In addition to helping fund the project, she’s a former Senate staffer who worked in Hart before Calder’s work was installed. Years after her time in the Senate was over, her husband Jon wanted to show her the sculpture, now filling the space she used to walk through every day.

But when the two arrived, the clouds weren’t hanging from the ceiling like they were supposed to be. He called up Rower, who was a friend of his, and said he wanted to get them back to how Calder intended. On Wednesday, the three of them stood together in Hart, looking up.

Technological and engineering advancements allowed for newer, lighter clouds to be built and be safe to hang from the ceiling.

“Before it was like a bulb, it looked like a hoagie sandwich, and now it looks just really sharp, like a razor cutting through space, which was Calder’s intention,” Rower said.

According to Rower, it involved laser-measuring the original model of Mountains and Clouds sitting in a glass case nearby in the Hart atrium. The new clouds, he said, are made of carbon fiber.

“These are giant things up in the air, and they’re just so gentle and subtle,” he said.

Younger Hill staffers don’t know a time with clouds. But for those who have spent decades in the building, it was a special moment to see them spin, as Lankford told the crowd.

“I can’t tell you how many tour groups that I’ve walked through this building and I pointed to this, and I said it’s only half there, and would take them over to the little model that’s right over here, and say this is what it’s supposed to look like,” said the senator, a former Hill staffer himself.

Standing under his grandfather’s sculpture, Rower found himself quoting the man responsible for it all.

“I find that everything I do, if it is made for a particular spot, is more successful,” he said, gazing up at it.

Some hotels are designed solely as places to sleep at night while you are traveling. Others, however, are meant to be a part of your travel experience. Unless I am truly checking in for a quick overnight stay, I always seek out the latter. That mindset is exactly what led me to Palihotel Hollywood on a recent visit to Los Angeles.

Palihotel Hollywood is one of more than 20 boutique properties under the Palisociety umbrella; a collection of independently branded hotels that prioritize design, connection and individuality. These include Palihouse, Palihotel, Le Petit Pali, ARRIVE by Palisociety and a handful of independently branded properties. Earlier this year, several Palisociety properties joined the Marriott Bonvoy ecosystem as part of a larger partnership between Design Hotels and Marriott.

"Design Hotels and Marriott Bonvoy give us the best of both worlds," Palisociety founder Avi Brosh told me in an interview about the partnership. "We stay fully independent in how our hotels look, feel and operate, and we gain access to one of the largest and most loyal traveler communities in the world. For Bonvoy members, it means they can earn and use their points at a hotel that feels genuinely personal and local. For us, it means introducing Palisociety to travelers who might never have found us otherwise."

Palihotel Hollywood is located just two blocks from iconic Hollywood landmarks such as the Chinese Theatre and the Hollywood Walk of Fame. The hotel's walkability and quick access to the highway made it an easy choice for our California home base, but it was the way I felt while I was there that made it memorable.

The hotel is a fully renovated 1958 motor lodge that retains its original appeal, making it feel right at home on Sunset Boulevard.

"[At Palihotel Hollywood], we leaned into that history rather than erasing it. The dark green facade, striped awnings, the checkerboard pool deck and Benny’s on the Blvd all are meant to belong to this hotel and this stretch of Hollywood. You won’t find them anywhere else," Brosh said.

As soon as I stepped into the lobby, I felt transported to Hollywood's golden age. I'm about the furthest thing from a celebrity looking for a secluded hideaway, but if I were, I would have found it here.

Through the lobby's back doors, I found the hotel's secluded courtyard. Green and white striped loungers with peach-hued umbrellas for shade surrounded the pool. The pool deck was bursting with greenery, which made it feel even more homelike.

Back inside, there is a cozy bar behind the front desk for afternoon and evening drinks, a seating area for guests to commune and Benny's on the Blvd, the hotel's restaurant that serves breakfast, lunch, afternoon snacks, coffee, beer, wine and cocktails. You can dine at the counter or by the pool to soak up the California sunshine.

Each of the hotel's small, intimate spaces adds to the neighborhood feel, a quality consistent across the brand. All Palisociety hotels have fewer than 150 rooms, with Palihotel Hollywood clocking in at 74 rooms and suites.

"Each of our hotels is completely unique, inspired by the individual spaces we inhabit and the communities we call home," Brosh said. "What stays consistent across every Palisociety property is the sensibility: warm, layered interiors that feel collected over time, thoughtful in-room touches, a social heart where guests actually want to gather, and hospitality that feels relaxed and personal rather than scripted. Every hotel should feel like it could only exist where it is, while still feeling unmistakably ours," he added.

Each Palisociety property has its own personality, with custom details and design touches that reflect its locale. Palihotel Hollywood, for example, leans into that vintage Hollywood charm throughout the public spaces and guest rooms.

The hotel offers king, queen and two double-bed rooms, pool-view rooms with patios or balconies overlooking the courtyard and interior "night owl" rooms with no exterior windows.

My room had plush fabrics, light-colored walls and furnishings with jewel-toned accent pieces like the headboard and loveseat, marble bathrooms and retro touches like a Smeg minifridge. From a practical perspective, I appreciated the Nespresso coffee machine, nightstands on both sides of the bed, in-room steamer — and loved the touch of Diptyque bath products.

Marriott Bonvoy members get many of the same benefits at Palisociety properties as they would elsewhere. These include the ability to earn and redeem points and redeem free night awards. Where Palisociety and other Design Hotels differ is in the elite benefits.

Elite members still earn bonus points on stays and can receive a welcome gift of points. Room upgrades are subject to availability, as is late checkout. Benefits like lounge access, nightly upgrade awards, discounted member rates, mobile check-in and key and similar perks are excluded for Design Hotels.

A one-night stay at Palihotel Hollywood starts at around $185 or 43,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night.

When I asked Brosh how Palihotels keeps nightly rates reasonable while offering a bespoke experience, he told me, "We spend money where guests feel it and save it where they don’t. That means investing in the things you touch and use every day, like great linens, good lighting, Diptyque in the bathroom, a real coffee setup, and being disciplined about everything else. We also love working with existing buildings that already have soul, which lets us put our effort into character instead of square footage. Good design doesn’t have to be expensive. It has to be considered."

Palihotel Hollywood perfectly encapsulates the Palisociety ethos to "enhance the experiences of our guests and our communities by creating one-of-a-kind places filled with interesting people, friendly staff and trusty service."

If you are looking for an exceptional stay that feels comfortable and welcoming, where you can earn or redeem Marriott Bonvoy points and enjoy some of your elite status benefits, you'll feel right at home with Palisociety.

#5974. Rove Gives You 1,500 Free Miles Just For Signing Up—Plus 5,000 More On Your First $500 Hotel Booking

Rove is offering 1,500 free miles just for signing up. You don’t have to book a trip, buy anything, or complete any other transaction. I specifically asked about an activity requirement, and Rove confirmed that new members get the miles instantly. I’ve written quite a bit about Rove, and asked them to improve the offer available through my link. This is three times the standard 500-mile referral signup bonus. Just like normal referrals, I receive Rove Miles when someone signs up through this link. It doesn’t cost you anything. In fact it gets you much more than not using this link. They’ve also created a hotel booking code for readers: 1,500 miles for joining: Use this link to create your new account. There’s no purchase requirement. 5,000 additional miles on your first hotel booking of $500 or more: Enter promo code VFTW when booking through Rove. A new member who uses both offers would earn 6,500 bonus miles, on top of the normal miles from their qualifying hotel booking. You can also just take the signup miles. And 5,000 miles on a $500 booking is twice what Rove offered at that spending level during its May promotion. What You Can Do With These Miles Rove is a free rewards program that lets you earn miles from hotel and flight bookings, online shopping, dining and gift cards. You don’t have to apply for a credit card, and you can earn rewards from the card you use to pay as well. Their transfer partners include familiar programs like Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. They also have programs that are harder to access through the major bank currencies, including Lufthansa Miles & More (for better availability of business and first class awards), Japan Airlines Mileage Bank (better availability of awards, lower prices on partner awards), Air India Maharaja Club (United awards starting at just 3,500 points) and Copa ConnectMiles (Emirates awards with no fuel surcharges). Rove has a 2,000-mile minimum for partner transfers. You don’t need a hotel stay to earn additional miles. I’ve covered Rove’s dining program and instant gift card rewards, and just wrote about its personalized shopping offers of up to 25 miles per dollar. When The Hotel Bonus Makes Sense You can also redeem Rove Miles directly for travel. As I wrote last month, I can usually get around 1.5 cents apiece redeeming them for hotel stays that still earn hotel points and elite status credit. Using that benchmark, the 5,000-mile hotel bonus is worth about $75 toward travel. On a qualifying $500 booking, that’s an extra 15% in value before the booking’s regular rewards. Expressed another way, the promo adds 10 miles per dollar at exactly $500 in qualifying spend. I’ve been particularly interested in Rove’s Loyalty Eligible hotel rates. There are two different kinds of bookings to compare: Loyalty Eligible rates generally earn 5 Rove miles per dollar, while preserving eligibility for the hotel’s own points, elite night credit and status benefits. The hotel charges your card, which can make paying with that chain’s credit card attractive. Rove Rates can offer more Rove miles, with the site advertising up to 25 per dollar, but generally give up the hotel loyalty program earnings and benefits. That tradeoff is easier at an independent hotel where you wouldn’t earn chain points anyway. I’d take the free signup miles. For the hotel offer, enter VFTW and consider the rate you’re selecting before booking for the 5,000-mile bonus. #5973. Mamdani’s ‘Affordability’ Deception

It turns out affordability and socialism are incompatible. Who knew?

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani holds up bananas as he speaks at a food distribution center in Brooklyn, N.Y., July 27, 2026.

New Yorkers are coming to terms with the unenviable conditions they’ve voted themselves into, with some experiencing sticker shock and a commensurate degree of buyer’s remorse. Who could blame them? The response from Democrats to the public’s frustrations should only further reinforce the unavoidable conclusion that New Yorkers have populated city government with neophytes and ignoramuses.

New York Times reporter Emma Fitzsimmons could not have anticipated the garment-rending apoplexy that her social media post would inspire in city officials. Nevertheless, she fulfilled her reportorial duties when, after completing her Amazon.com purchase of a children’s liquid vitamin, she encountered this message from the online retailer: “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order,” it read. “Act now to protect low prices.”

Noah Rothman is a senior writer at National Review. His third book, Blood and Progress: A Century of Left-Wing Violence, was published by Hachette in May 2026.

National Review Institute is a non-profit, 501(c)(3), journalistic think tank that preserves and promotes William F. Buckley Jr.’s legacy, supports the National Review mission, and advances the principles of a free society through educational and outreach programs. All contributions to it are deductible for income, gift, and estate tax purposes. EIN# 13-3649537

Rove now has more than 20 transfer options, including Japan Airlines Mileage Bank, Air France-KLM Flying Blue, Qatar Airways Privilege Club, Air Canada Aeroplan, Lufthansa Miles & More, Qantas Frequent Flyer and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club.

If you don't have any Rove miles, you can earn 1,500 miles at no cost right now just by signing up through this link. You can also earn an additional 5,000 miles when making your first hotel booking over $500 as a new user with the code "BRIANKELLY500."

Related: The best ways to redeem Rove miles, including flights to Europe from just 88 miles

We only recommend transferring points or miles if you have a short-term plan to use them. Transfers are irreversible, and you don’t want to be stuck with thousands of points or miles in a program you have little use for.

If you don’t have a specific redemption in mind but still want to earn points or miles, you’re likely better off earning rewards through card welcome bonuses and everyday spending.

We always recommend verifying award availability before transferring your rewards.

When a program with a transferable currency offers a transfer bonus, it’s important to run the numbers to determine whether it is worthwhile.

Generally, you won’t want to transfer your points or miles unless you have a specific redemption in mind. After all, a large part of the value of transferable points and miles comes from their flexibility, which you’ll give up when you convert them to a partner’s currency. However, a transfer bonus can help you get more value from your points and miles if you frequently use a partner program or plan to redeem them soon.

#5971. Rove Launches Elite Status With Third Night Free Hotel Awards—Will This Turn Deal Chasers Into Loyal Customers?

Rove is launching elite status with a third night free on eligible hotel awards, and top tier Diamond members get two free nights on a six night stay. You can qualify through travel bookings, shopping and dining, without holding a particular credit card. The benefits can make Rove more rewarding. They may also bean attempt to address the problem I’ve had with the business from the beginning: when you attract customers by giving them the best deal, what keeps them around when somebody else offers more? How Rove’s New Status Program Works Rove Status launches November 23, 2026. Everyone starts as a Member, and there are three earned tiers. You need both qualifying miles and qualifying transactions during a calendar year: Status Qualifying Miles Qualifying Transactions Gold 50,000 5 Platinum 125,000 10 Diamond 250,000 20 Qualifying activity from earlier in 2026 counts retroactively, and status earned in 2026 lasts through December 31, 2027. Rove clarified what counts: Transaction earnings count, including elevated rates and status bonuses. Miles associated with paid travel bookings, shopping, gift cards and dining qualify. That includes purchased Miles Boost earnings. Flat bonuses don’t count. An offer of 2,500 bonus miles for spending $500 won’t add those 2,500 miles to your status progress, although the qualifying purchase and its ordinary earnings still count. Referrals, transfers, customer support credits and other miles unrelated to a cash transaction don’t count. Pure award redemptions don’t earn qualifying miles or transactions either. Rove makes an exception for miles + cash bookings. Shopping, dining and gift cards count based on the purchase date. Travel counts when it’s completed: hotel checkout or the last flight of a multi-segment trip. Booking a hotel in December for a January checkout won’t help with 2026 status. Late posting doesn’t move activity into the wrong year. If a December purchase posts in January, it still counts toward 2026 qualification, and Rove can award the resulting status after the new year begins. The spending required depends on how quickly you earn qualifying miles. At an average of 10 qualifying miles per dollar, Gold takes $5,000, Platinum $12,500, and Diamond $25,000. At 25 qualifying miles per dollar, Diamond takes $10,000. At 5, it takes $50,000. You still need the required number of qualifying transactions. And once you earn status, the extra miles from eligible elite earning bonuses help you reach the next tier or requalify. Here are the announced benefits: Benefit Gold Platinum Diamond Free night on eligible Rove Rate awards Fifth night Fourth night Third night Discount on eligible paid hotel rates, excluding Loyalty Eligible 5% 8% 10% Additional shopping miles per dollar at select brands Up to 5 Up to 8 Up to 10 Paid Miles Boost limit Up to 12x Up to 15x Up to 20x Rove’s partner transfer minimum 1,500 miles 1,000 miles No minimum Extra transfer bonus during eligible promotions None listed 10 percentage points 15 percentage points Customer support Gold priority Platinum priority Diamond priority and Diamond Desk All three earned tiers also offer parental leave: new parents can extend their status expiration by 12 months. Rove says additional partner benefits are coming. The Free Hotel Night Is The Biggest Benefit — With An Important Limitation A third night free can be substantial, and Rove confirms a six night Diamond stay receives two free nights. The deduction uses the average nightly price, so a cheaper third night doesn’t shrink the benefit. On a three or six night Diamond award, the eligible award cost falls by a third. Platinum saves 25% on a four night award and Gold saves 20% on a five night award. Rove says the free night calculation excludes only fees due at the hotel, such as resort fees or locally collected taxes. (Those charges remain payable.) That also makes each mile worth more. A third off the miles required means 50% more value per mile. And I generally get about 1.5 cents per Rove Mile as it is. But both the free award nights and the paid hotel discounts exclude Loyalty Eligible bookings. Those have been my favorite use of Rove miles. The free nights apply to Rove Rate awards, which are going to be third party bookings (may not earn points, status credit or receive status benefits). With Loyalty Eligible stays, you can redeem Rove miles and still earn hotel points and elite night credit, while receiving your hotel status benefits. Rove Rate bookings don’t earn those hotel points or nights, and don’t guarantee your hotel elite benefits. I’d be most interested in the free night benefit at independent hotels, or on stays where I don’t have valuable hotel status to give up. A discounted three or six night award could be a much better use of miles than the same stay was before. Rove explains that it can’t offer the paid hotel discount on Loyalty Eligible rates because the hotel is the merchant of record and Rove doesn’t control the pricing. I’d note that commissions are lower, too, so it would also be costlier to offer. Extra Transfer Bonuses And Shopping Bonuses The extra transfer bonuses apply on top of eligible existing promotions, and Rove confirms they’re additive. A 40% promotion becomes 50% for Platinum and 55% for Diamond. At a partner with a normal 1:1 ratio, transferring 10,000 Rove miles during that offer would yield 14,000 partner miles ordinarily, 15,000 for Platinum, or 15,500 for Diamond. There’s no standing 15% Diamond bonus on every transfer. The shopping bonuses mean additional miles per dollar. Diamond’s maximum is 10 extra miles per dollar at select brands, rather than multiplying the ordinary earning rate by ten. These bonuses aren’t available on everything you buy, but where offered they improve both your redeemable points-earn and status progress. Lower transfer minimums are useful for topping off an airline account. Rove’s ordinary minimum is 2,000 miles, though individual partners can have their own minimums or increments. Removing Rove’s minimum is a nice convenience. Rove Needs Customers Who Come Back I’ve written about Rove’s customer challenge. An airline starts with passengers who need its flights. A hotel company starts with guests who need rooms in its locations. Rove has to persuade people to use its platform for purchases they were already making. They’ve done that by frequently being more rewarding than competitors. That’s attracted attention and business, but it also attracts the loyalty equivalent of hot money. Customers compare offers, take the richest one, and potentially. Status gives the next transaction value beyond the miles it earns immediately. Someone approaching Gold might choose Rove even when another portal offers a little more. Someone who already has Diamond may keep earning because they want enough miles for another discounted three night stay. And even without doing the math, people like reaching a tier and dislike losing it. The transaction requirements push customers beyond one big purchase. Rove’s expansion into dining, shopping and an app gives customers more reasons to return between trips. Status gives those activities a common target. And while a rich acquisition offer pays someone who might never come back, a status discount generally requires another booking before Rove incurs the cost. Some members won’t use it. Rove can direct more of its rewards spending toward customers who return, instead of having to offer the biggest public bonus to everyone. The hotel award benefit also encourages members to redeem within Rove instead of transferring their miles to an airline. That may be cheaper where Rove has favorable hotel inventory costs. I’d Like To See More Than Bigger Rebates What’s largely missing is the experience of being treated differently. An airline can give you a better seat that would otherwise go empty. A hotel can upgrade you to an unsold suite. The customer may value that far more than it costs to deliver. Rove doesn’t control those seats and rooms, so promising similar treatment would require agreements with partners. Rove is giving better customer service with status – I asked what the Diamond Desk actually does, and they shared it provides maximum customer support priority and a dedicated email address. Rove is doing the rewarding part well, but they haven’t quite yet figured out recognition which is just as much a part of loyalty. A third off the miles required means 50% more value per mile. And I generally get about 1.5 cents per Rove Mile as it is.

But both the free award nights and the paid hotel discounts exclude Loyalty Eligible bookings. Those have been my favorite use of Rove miles. The free nights apply to Rove Rate awards, which are going to be third party bookings (may not earn points, status credit or receive status benefits).

With Loyalty Eligible stays, you can redeem Rove miles and still earn hotel points and elite night credit, while receiving your hotel status benefits. Rove Rate bookings don’t earn those hotel points or nights, and don’t guarantee your hotel elite benefits.

I’d be most interested in the free night benefit at independent hotels, or on stays where I don’t have valuable hotel status to give up. A discounted three or six night award could be a much better use of miles than the same stay was before. Rove explains that it can’t offer the paid hotel discount on Loyalty Eligible rates because the hotel is the merchant of record and Rove doesn’t control the pricing. I’d note that commissions are lower, too, so it would also be costlier to offer.

The extra transfer bonuses apply on top of eligible existing promotions, and Rove confirms they’re additive. A 40% promotion becomes 50% for Platinum and 55% for Diamond. At a partner with a normal 1:1 ratio, transferring 10,000 Rove miles during that offer would yield 14,000 partner miles ordinarily, 15,000 for Platinum, or 15,500 for Diamond. There’s no standing 15% Diamond bonus on every transfer. The shopping bonuses mean additional miles per dollar. Diamond’s maximum is 10 extra miles per dollar at select brands, rather than multiplying the ordinary earning rate by ten. These bonuses aren’t available on everything you buy, but where offered they improve both your redeemable points-earn and status progress. Lower transfer minimums are useful for topping off an airline account. Rove’s ordinary minimum is 2,000 miles, though individual partners can have their own minimums or increments. Removing Rove’s minimum is a nice convenience. Rove Needs Customers Who Come Back I’ve written about Rove’s customer challenge. An airline starts with passengers who need its flights. A hotel company starts with guests who need rooms in its locations. Rove has to persuade people to use its platform for purchases they were already making. They’ve done that by frequently being more rewarding than competitors. That’s attracted attention and business, but it also attracts the loyalty equivalent of hot money. Customers compare offers, take the richest one, and potentially. Status gives the next transaction value beyond the miles it earns immediately. Someone approaching Gold might choose Rove even when another portal offers a little more. Someone who already has Diamond may keep earning because they want enough miles for another discounted three night stay. And even without doing the math, people like reaching a tier and dislike losing it. The transaction requirements push customers beyond one big purchase. Rove’s expansion into dining, shopping and an app gives customers more reasons to return between trips. Status gives those activities a common target. And while a rich acquisition offer pays someone who might never come back, a status discount generally requires another booking before Rove incurs the cost. Some members won’t use it. Rove can direct more of its rewards spending toward customers who return, instead of having to offer the biggest public bonus to everyone. The hotel award benefit also encourages members to redeem within Rove instead of transferring their miles to an airline. That may be cheaper where Rove has favorable hotel inventory costs. I’d Like To See More Than Bigger Rebates What’s largely missing is the experience of being treated differently. An airline can give you a better seat that would otherwise go empty. A hotel can upgrade you to an unsold suite. The customer may value that far more than it costs to deliver. Rove doesn’t control those seats and rooms, so promising similar treatment would require agreements with partners. Rove is giving better customer service with status – I asked what the Diamond Desk actually does, and they shared it provides maximum customer support priority and a dedicated email address. Rove is doing the rewarding part well, but they haven’t quite yet figured out recognition which is just as much a part of loyalty.
