You continue to highlight what I’ll call the Citi Strata Elite problem. I like Rove. It’s a nice program. There’s real value there. But there’s no pot of gold at the end of the rainbow in terms of making my travel experience easier (airline status / more than 4 lounge passes). So it’s hard to get too excited about the program in general, even though it potentially offers some really good value. Versus, say, AA Hotels where I can get 12x automatically on the spend plus offers that get me tons additional miles/LP towards status.

The number of transactions is a bit meaningless when you can buy $5 gift cards. But the spend requirement is real here – if you are assuming an average of 20x miles from your Rove spend (which could be high but who knows) that’s $12.5k in spend to get top status. If you are regularly staying places three nights or longer, could be a valuable benefit as well.

But would I rather have free access to MCE/extra legroom seating versus using a hotel free night stay benefit a few times a year? Probably! But that’s just me, based on my travel patterns. YMMV.

I’ve been using Rove but also finding a lot of issues. – Almost always, the offer they show me “no longer availabe” when I go to check out and a new offer is shown instead. – There are pricing games going on, where for examples, taxes change dramatically if you and or remove breakfast or whether it’s refundable. (The taxes in this case are not related to the difference in cost.) – I was booking something the other day and they kept declining the transactions. But Chase swears they didn’t get those transactions. – And what I consider the worst thing, the photos and descriptions they have on rooms often does not match what you actually get. They tend to put the same photos on multiple room types, so if you don’t know this and don’t verify on other sites you get screwed. – I find there overall presentation of hotels terrible too, so you basically have to find what you want elsewhere and search here just for price. It’s definitely not a one stop shop. So overall, I’m still not sure it’s worth it.

#5969. Progressive advocates call on House Democrats to force Cuba vote

Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., is the sponsor of a Cuba war powers resolution filed in May. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Progressive advocates are urging House Democrats to force a vote during the lame-duck session on a resolution aimed at preventing war against Cuba, arguing the issue is too urgent to wait until Democrats control the chamber next year.

“The Cuban people are suffering and dying, and cannot afford further months of inaction,” 50 progressive groups wrote to Democratic House leaders in a letter dated Wednesday. “In the midterm elections, U.S. voters resoundingly rejected a foreign policy of war and domination, and made clear their desire for Congress to act forcefully to rein in the Trump administration.

Holding a vote would demonstrate that Democrats recognize the urgency facing the Cuban people, and would help set the tone for an assertive agenda of peace, diplomacy and respect for international law in the 120th Congress, the letter added.

At issue is a war powers resolution introduced in May by Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, D-N.Y., and House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., that would call on the president “to remove the United States Armed Forces from hostilities within or against Cuba, unless explicitly authorized by a declaration of war or a specific authorization for use of military force.”

The letter was sent to House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Meeks and House Rules Committee ranking member Jim McGovern, D-Mass. It was signed by prominent anti-war groups such as Win Without War, Just Foreign Policy, the Friends Committee on National Legislation, Indivisible and Code Pink.

Advocates are frustrated that House Democrats have not forced a vote on a Cuba war powers resolution even as they have forced multiple war powers votes on Iran and see it as an example of leadership that is at odds with the progressive wing of the party. One advocate who requested anonymity to speak candidly said it’s their understanding Democratic leaders are hesitant to make potentially vulnerable Florida members of the caucus vote on the issue.

Spokespeople for Jeffries and Meeks did not respond to requests for comment Wednesday on whether Democrats will force a vote before the end of the year, what their reasoning is if they don’t and whether they plan to bring up a vote next year.

Senate Democrats sought to force a vote on a similar resolution earlier this year, but Republicans in that chamber successfully derailed the effort. Senate Republicans raised a point of order that the resolution was not entitled to privileged status under the War Powers Resolution since U.S. troops aren't actively engaged in combat against Cuba. The point of order was sustained in a mostly party-line vote of 51-47.

Senate Democrats later introduced another Cuba war powers resolution, which they have not tried to force a vote on and have not signaled they will do so before the end of the year.

The resolutions have come amid several veiled threats from President Donald Trump suggesting eventual military action against Cuba.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt last week when asked if he would order the use of military force against Cuba.

“Frankly, I’d love to be able to do it for the people, for the Cubans that came and were treated really badly, and they came to America,” Trump said, adding he would “certainly consider” taking military action.

Trump’s comments are on top of a pressure campaign his administration has been waging against Cuba. Since January, the United States has imposed a blockade of oil shipments to the island, causing fuel shortages that have led to lengthy blackouts and aggravated an economic crisis.

While the Senate vote in April did not go Democrats’ way, advocates still saw it as sending a strong message.

“Despite falling short of the majority, this was among the strongest votes in congressional history against the use of blockades, and one of the most important stands Congress has taken against U.S. economic sanctions toward Cuba in over six decades,” the letter from progressive organizations said. “The House should take a similarly forceful action at this crucial moment.”

The House vote, even if successful, would be largely symbolic since the measure Democrats can force a vote on is a concurrent resolution. Concurrent resolutions are widely considered to be nonbinding even if cleared by both chambers of Congress since they do not get a presidential signature, though anti-war advocates dispute that applies to war powers.

The progressive groups in their letter called for “decisive leadership” in forcing a vote on the issue.

“Across the political spectrum,” the letter said, “Americans do not want another regime change war, nor an open-ended, nation-building project abroad based on false pretenses — especially not when escalation risks exposing the United States to new national security risks, placing US servicemembers in harm’s way, stoking regional instability, and becoming the latest chapter in a long history of harmful U.S. regional policies that have fueled mass migration to U.S. shores.”

#5968. American Airlines Will Displace Philadelphia Pilots—Blames Union For Rejecting A321XLR Staffing Deal

American Airlines says a “significant number” of Philadelphia pilots will be displaced from their current positions after their union’s board rejected a deal on staffing Airbus A321XLR flights to Europe. The airline is reopening a domestic Airbus pilot base and shrinking its international one for June 2027. That can change which trips pilots fly, the schedules they can hold, and potentially their commutes. American is blaming the union for rejecting what it calls an “objectively better path forward.” Aviation watchdog JonNYC shares the company’s message to pilots: When we publish our June 2027 vacancy announcement tomorrow, you will see that we are reopening a PHL A320 Domestic base (Section 17.S.1) and reducing the PHL A320 International base. This will, unfortunately, result in the displacement of a significant number of pilots from the PHL A320 International base (Section 17.D). The airline says it had agreed to a term sheet with the Allied Pilots Association, completed the contractual language, and expected a signed side agreement. The union’s board rejected it November 6. November 22, 2026 The dispute connects two things that don’t seem related at first blush: which pilots get lucrative extra trips, and how American makes sure its new Europe flights have qualified crews. I wrote in April about American’s new Aggressive Pick-up system. It gives pilots access to last-minute open trips on a first-come, first-served basis. Those trips can come with premium pay. Junior pilots gained access to flying that senior pilots had been accustomed to getting. That helps American cover flights and creates opportunities for junior pilots. It also takes income opportunities away from senior ones. The fight over “fixing” the system is largely about who gets the money. The union wanted seniority to count in those awards, along with priority for pilots based where the trip originates and fixes to message delays. American saw something it could trade for. The union’s September 18 negotiating update described the exchange: Pilots would get changes to the extra-trip pickup system. Seniority and in-base priority would play a role, and the parties would address problems with how trip opportunities reached pilots. American would get changes to monthly schedule bidding for its Europe operation. The airline wanted Atlantic Europe qualifications incorporated into its Preferential Bidding System, the software that builds pilots’ schedules. The memo calls this an “A320” issue because that’s the pilot fleet category, which includes the A321XLR. A pilot qualified to fly an Airbus domestically still needs the additional qualifications for this oceanic flying. “AE” means Atlantic Europe here. American needs the pilots qualified for those trips to be available to fly them. A large pool of Airbus pilots doesn’t solve the problem if the pilots who can fly to Europe are awarded domestic schedules, while pilots who haven’t completed the necessary training are entitled by seniority to the Europe trips. The union’s October 27 update explained limited changes to bidding rules for Airbus pilots in categories with current or future XLR Europe flying, paired with seniority protections in the qualification training plan. Pilots discussing the proposed agreement described the risk of qualified pilots being directed toward Europe trips or reserve assignments they wouldn’t otherwise choose, while unqualified pilots could lose access to trips their seniority would otherwise let them bid. Pilots across the airline could benefit from changes to extra-trip awards, while the scheduling concessions would fall on the Airbus pilots affected by Europe flying. And restoring seniority in those awards helps senior pilots at the expense of junior pilots who’ve been quick enough to claim the trips. There’s a distributional problem inside the union. Some pilots argued that the union was giving up too much: American needed flexibility for an important expansion, and the union should obtain more for it in broader contract negotiations. The union had also filed a grievance over American’s failure to implement the Line Check Pilot program from the 2023 agreement, so training capacity was already a point of contention. American’s response is to divide the Philadelphia Airbus pilot group. It will reopen a domestic category and reduce the international category. A smaller, separately staffed international group gives American a more manageable pool to qualify and schedule for Europe. That avoids needing the rejected changes to keep the existing group together. The airline is using the base and displacement provisions in its contract. Under the pilot contract, reductions in a bidding category generally displace the least senior pilots, with provisions for more senior pilots to volunteer. Displaced pilots exercise their seniority into other positions, which can set off further displacement. A pilot can remain in Philadelphia on the same aircraft family but have access to different trips and schedules. Others’ choices could mean changing bases, aircraft, or commuting arrangements. American’s 2027 Europe plans include Philadelphia–Porto beginning March 28 and Philadelphia–Vienna beginning May 6, both using the A321XLR. I toured the aircraft before it entered service. It has just 155 seats: 20 business class suites, 12 premium economy seats, and 123 in coach. American can offer a premium product across the Atlantic with fewer seats to fill than on a Boeing 787. That opens up routes and seasons where a larger aircraft is harder to justify. I liked the operational benefit of making last-minute trips available to pilots willing to fly them. Getting an airplane out on time has value, and senior pilots losing priority for some extra income standing in the way of operational reliability has been a key cause of Delta’s operational meltdowns. Management calls the rejected deal objectively better. That depends on whose schedule and income you’re counting. A senior pilot seeking premium trips and a Philadelphia Airbus pilot facing restrictions on monthly bidding are different pilots gaining benefits and incurring costs. Much of a union’s role is trading off the same or better total benefits between its members, rather than getting the best possible overall deal from the employer. And union politics play an important role, especially as the American Airlines pilots union remains in the midst of drama over whether it will stay independent or join the larger Air Line Pilots Association. It has just 155 seats: 20 business class suites, 12 premium economy seats, and 123 in coach. American can offer a premium product across the Atlantic with fewer seats to fill than on a Boeing 787. That opens up routes and seasons where a larger aircraft is harder to justify.

I liked the operational benefit of making last-minute trips available to pilots willing to fly them. Getting an airplane out on time has value, and senior pilots losing priority for some extra income standing in the way of operational reliability has been a key cause of Delta’s operational meltdowns.

Management calls the rejected deal objectively better. That depends on whose schedule and income you’re counting. A senior pilot seeking premium trips and a Philadelphia Airbus pilot facing restrictions on monthly bidding are different pilots gaining benefits and incurring costs. Much of a union’s role is trading off the same or better total benefits between its members, rather than getting the best possible overall deal from the employer. And union politics play an important role, especially as the American Airlines pilots union remains in the midst of drama over whether it will stay independent or join the larger Air Line Pilots Association.

The real-world value of choosing the right credit cards for your everyday spending We frequently tout the incredible value you can get from top rewards credit cards — from bonus categories to welcome offers, lucrative benefits to monthly statement credits.

But exactly how much value can you get from matching the right credit cards to your spending habits?

Well, we recently set out to answer this very question.

We challenged three American households with a simple question: Can you make the money you’re already spending work harder for you?

Mollie and Kevin were up first. The pair recently moved in together ahead of their wedding, and they’re working through how to combine their finances while also saving for their dream honeymoon to Thailand and Vietnam. Both had travel rewards cards before the challenge, but they weren’t coordinating their purchases.

Plus, they were still using debit cards for some everyday expenses.

In short, they had room for improvement in how they made the most of the cards in their wallets.

They started by sitting down to map out their spending habits, which uncovered three primary categories being spread across multiple cards, without any rhyme or reason:

Plus, they had some major wedding expenses coming up, which gave them a great opportunity to snag a new card with a lucrative welcome bonus.

By coordinating their household spending, closing duplicate cards and opening a new one for the welcome offer, they’re now earning more from the same purchases they were already making.

The remaining balance of the catering bill for their wedding alone hit the minimum spending required to earn the welcome offer, and when all was said and done, the couple took home 120,000 points — worth nearly $2,500 based on TPG’s most recent valuations.

Next stop for Mollie and Kevin? Southeast Asia.

Next, we meet Amy, a single mom of two daughters in Maryland. She’s been earning rewards on her favorite hotel cobranded card for years, using it for basically every purchase she could — from utilities to groceries to clothing. She’s racked up nearly 400,000 points in the process, which have come in handy as her daughters have begun traveling for dance competitions.

However, she was concerned her hotel loyalty meant she was sacrificing some value. Could she shift some of her spending to a new card to diversify her rewards?

With back-to-school shopping and dance classes making up the bulk of her spending in the next month, she opted to add a new card to her wallet that offered solid rewards on all purchases — along with some easy-to-use statement credits.

And a large home repair bill accelerated her progress toward earning the welcome bonus — a great way to make the best of an unexpected expense.

She’s still keeping her old hotel card open, since it features a low annual fee, and she’ll still want to earn (and redeem) those points when it works. However, the rewards on her new card give her the newfound flexibility she didn’t have originally.

“I really had tunnel vision with the hotel points,” she admitted. “I was leaving money on the table."

Our final household focuses on Denver, a travel enthusiast who was thrown a pair of major life curveballs last year when her grandfather passed away, and her mom lost her job (and thus her source of income). She moved back home to help, and travel (understandably) shifted to the back burner.

While Denver charged many purchases to her favorite travel rewards card, she had other purchases pulled straight from her bank account. She was also worried that putting everything on her credit card would encourage her to spend more. However, there was a key opportunity in her new role as a caretaker: focusing on everyday spending rather than travel rewards.

Denver opted for a new cash-back credit card with bonuses at grocery stores, on streaming services and at gas stations. It even offered a one-time $300 cash-back bonus. These rewards can immediately help offset her household bills, like medication costs, be saved for an unexpected expense, or even go toward a future getaway with her family.

She’s continuing to pay her statement balance in full and on time, so it’s not about spending more; it’s about smarter spending based on her current situation.

After just a month, Denver is tracking toward nearly $1,500 in cash-back rewards in the first year — just by being more intentional with her everyday spending.

One of the most common questions we get here at TPG is, “What’s the best credit card for me?” And there’s a simple answer: “It depends.”

Everyone’s situation is unique, so there’s no one-size-fits-all approach to maximizing your everyday spending. And these three households demonstrate that exact phenomenon.

One went with a new travel card to maximize their wedding purchases. Another opted for a flexible rewards card to diversify her earnings. And the third focused on a cash-back card to support her family’s bottom line.

All of them are now getting even more value from the purchases they were already making.

This is the power of matching the cards in your wallet to your daily spending — while keeping a keen eye on earning the rewards that work best for you.

Don’t miss out on the chance to make your everyday purchases work harder for you. Analyze where you’re spending your money today, so you can unlock even more value tomorrow.

#5966. Three Women Argued Over An American Airlines Delay—Then Got Kicked Off And Blamed For Missed Connections

Three women were escorted off an American Airlines flight from Knoxville to Charlotte on Saturday night after an argument with a flight attendant, costing passengers their connections. Retired Kansas City Royals vice president Mike Swanson called them “princesses” in his story of the November 21 incident. The plane was already late getting to Knoxville, before the women could have held it up. Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026 In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. The flight attendant told the women they were ready to depart and to fasten their seat belts. The exchange escalated: The three got loud and the attendant wasn’t having it. They gone. Video shows two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson says three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte. Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. Last year I wrote about an American Airlines passenger who told a flight attendant to shut up during the safety demonstration and wound up getting the plane sent back to the gate. It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m. Charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night. However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip. The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument. (HT: @bags) Topics on this pageAir travelAmerican AirlinesAmerican Eagle OutfittersBombardierBombardier CRJ900CharlotteKnoxvillePSA Airlines+6 more More From View from the Wing

Mike Swanson’s video of passengers being escorted off his flight — November 22, 2026

In a follow-up on Twitter, Swanson explains that one woman complained to the flight attendant about how long it had taken to board. The flight attendant told the women they were ready to depart and to fasten their seat belts. The exchange escalated:

The three got loud and the attendant wasn’t having it. They gone.

Video shows two women walking toward the front with their belongings, followed by a uniformed officer. Swanson says three were removed. He says several passengers missed connections in Charlotte.

Yelling at a flight attendant because your flight is late is a lousy strategy for getting home sooner. Last year I wrote about an American Airlines passenger who told a flight attendant to shut up during the safety demonstration and wound up getting the plane sent back to the gate.

It appears this was American Eagle flight 5675 on November 21, operated by PSA Airlines using a Bombardier CRJ900, registration N557NN. That flight was scheduled to leave Knoxville at 8:04 p.m. and arrive in Charlotte at 9:28 p.m. It took off at 9:57 p.m. and landed at 10:34 p.m.

Charlotte is a particularly bad place to lose your connection buffer. I’ve written about how arriving on a regional jet can mean waiting for a valet checked bag and then making a long walk from Concourse E. A late evening arrival also leaves fewer chances to recover with another flight that night.

However, that aircraft’s inbound flight from Charlotte didn’t land in Knoxville until 8:35 p.m. It was supposed to have arrived at 7:34 p.m. The plane was still arriving 31 minutes after it should have departed on its next trip.

The women weren’t responsible for the original delay. Removing them may have used up whatever chance remained to make his connection, but we don’t whether he’d have made it without the argument.

#5965. American Airlines Loses O’Hare Gate Appeal—But United’s Plan To Drive It Out Of Chicago Is Failing

American Airlines just lost its appeal to undo Chicago O’Hare’s gate reshuffle. But it’s already bought two gates from Spirit, earned back gate space through its own growth, and survived United’s effort to push it out of Chicago. The airline’s position is stronger than when it sued, and judges haven’t finally decided whether the city broke its contract. The new ruling upholds the refusal to issue a preliminary injunction. The question of whether Chicago took American’s gates too early, after promising to give the airline a chance to grow into additional space first still hasn’t been resolved. I still think American has the better argument about the contract. I’ve also been skeptical from the beginning that they’d get an injunction, since money damages seemed possible. The November 19 appellate decision fits that distinction, although the trial judge’s preliminary reading of the contract was unfavorable to American. The judge accepted that Chicago made American an explicit promise The dispute goes back to the 2018 airport lease. United was getting gates freed up by Delta’s move to Terminal 5. American objected to widening United’s advantage, and Chicago agreed to three additional gates on the north side of the L concourse extension. The lease called for gate assignments following an attached map, with those assignments remaining in place for at least twelve months. American’s argument was that it needed to actually receive the promised capacity before that protected period could run. Otherwise United could grow using its additional gates while American waited for its own, and then the city would use the unequal flying to take gates away from American. The way gates work at Chicago O’Hare is that prior flying determines future gate space (or, technically, ‘linear frontage’). That’s the problem I identified when American first filed its lawsuit. The timing was part of the bargain that got American to support the redevelopment agreement in the first place. And the trial judget accepted that the city and American had agreed to tie the process to the three additional gates becoming operational: For purposes of this motion, that much—the Court has no doubt—was the deal. His position, though, is that the city’s fingers were crossed, suggesting that the explicit written commitment didn’t make it into the final lease, or at least that American couldn’t establish that it had: The language identifies completion of the Terminal 5 expansion and an airline’s relocation there as the triggers. It doesn’t separately name completion of American’s three gates. The additional gates appear on the map as common use space, which the city controls, rather than space reserved for American’s preferential use. The lease says it’s the complete agreement. The judge treated its language as unambiguous and excluded the earlier negotiations as a way to add a condition to it. American’s last additional gate became operational March 14, 2025. Under its reading, the protected year therefore ran through March 2026, and the next redetermination could begin April 1, 2027. Chicago instead treated the protected period as having begun in December 2023, allowing redistribution in 2025. The city’s reading is silly. The map is part of the signed agreement. Requiring the city to deliver the capacity shown there before starting a year of protected assignments doesn’t require inventing a promise outside the contract. And designating a gate common use doesn’t explain how a gate that isn’t operational can fulfill a promise intended to let an airline ramp up flying. Why American lost the injunction appeal The appellate court assumed American could satisfy the initial requirements for an injunction and still concluded that the harm from blocking the gate changes justified denying one. It was reviewing whether the trial judge abused his discretion, NOT deciding the contract dispute from scratch. American’s problem was that it didn’t establish losing the gates would destroy its Chicago hub. It planned to operate the same number of flights using fewer gates, with more flying at less attractive times and less room to recover from delays. That could cost money, make operations worse and harm passengers but it made the injury look measurable. That was my original point – that this would be a case for future damages rather than an injunction. Meanwhile, the other airlines had planned schedules around the redistribution. United projected more than 2,000 cancellations if it were blocked. That number was overblown but the court accepted that changing the arrangements would disrupt passengers, other airlines, and airport construction. And the expectation that American would win gates back in the next allocation (which it did) undercut the argument that it faced an irreversible decline. Timing hurt American, too. Chicago announced the redistribution in February 2025. American sued in May but didn’t request preliminary relief until July. By the September hearing, the October gate changes were imminent and preparations were well underway. American argued that the city shouldn’t get to invoke the hardships from correcting an agreement they deliberately broke. The appeals court rejected that approach because it saw a reasonable dispute over what the contract meant. In my view, Chicago (intentionally) muddied the contract issue enough to make it less clear. This decision doesn’t end American’s lawsuit. It upholds the denial of a preliminary injunction. The contract claims and potential damages are still unresolved. The court rejected the argument that implementation of the gate changes had made the appeal moot, since a court could still order an effective remedy. United’s strategy ran into the airport’s actual capacity Chicago seemed strongly inclined to help its hometown airline. United’s headquarters are valuable to the city, especially with rumors of a move to Denver hanging over the relationship. My coverage of the gate dispute even generated an angry phone call from Chicago “shadow mayor” Jason Lee. United saw a chance to turn American’s slow recovery from the pandemic into a permanent retreat. American had retired too many aircraft and couldn’t rebuild everywhere at once. Fewer Chicago departures meant fewer gates, which could make future growth harder. United CEO Scott Kirby tried to create pressure by talking up American’s Chicago losses and getting financial analysts to question why it should stay. United then announced additional flying on the morning of American’s earnings call, practically writing the questions for them. This was strategic flying. United clearly didn’t want all of that additional capacity. It wanted invesors to believe that any growth would be matched, so American couldn’t improve its gate position and would just lose more money trying. Kirby told analysts United would add “as many flights as are required” to protect its gate count. Then the Federal Aviation Administration intervened. The airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines were filing, especially with construction constraining movement on the ground. Its summer order capped scheduled arrivals and departures at 2,708 per day from May 17 through October 24. The government used approved summer 2025 schedules as its baseline. It rejected rewarding airlines for filing unrealistic 2026 schedules to improve their negotiating position. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff. The cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution. The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United. American needs Chicago to rebuild the business Kirby claims American loses so much money in Chicago that it should leave. Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its plans to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months. Topics on this pageAmerican AirlinesBreach of contractO'Hare International AirportPreliminary injunctionUnited AirlinesAAdvantageAlaska AirlinesChicagoCitibankCourtDelta Air LinesDenverFAALos AngelesNat PieperScott KirbySpirit AirlinesTWA Flight Center+13 more More From View from the Wing

Some version of those losses are real, created in part by the undersized schedule it had been flying. But the size and meaning of the losses get overstated. It requires assigning headquarters overhead to the hub that doesn’t disappear if the hub closes. And American would lose connecting traffic and credit card customers if that happened, too. American needs to be relevant in the largest markets where people spend heavily on cards. Retreating from Chicago would make AAdvantage less valuable to Chicago customers, and make its Citibank cards harder to sell and less attractive to spend on. Attributing credit card revenue to the customers and markets that generate it produces a different picture than spreading that revenue across flights throughout the network. That’s why Chicago belongs alongside American’s efforts to rebuild Los Angeles as gates return after construction, and its plans to bring Alaska Airlines into its Atlantic and Pacific joint ventures. They’re working to regain relevance in the largest spend markets in the country. The Chicago fight has also given employees something to rally around. In the post-earnings employee meeting I covered in January, Chief Commercial Officer Nat Pieper called United the “common enemy” and made it out to be a battle for loyalty and credit card performance. He reported roughly 20% growth in loyalty enrollments, card acquisitions, and local market share over the preceding nine months. The dispute goes back to the 2018 airport lease. United was getting gates freed up by Delta’s move to Terminal 5. American objected to widening United’s advantage, and Chicago agreed to three additional gates on the north side of the L concourse extension.

The lease called for gate assignments following an attached map, with those assignments remaining in place for at least twelve months. American’s argument was that it needed to actually receive the promised capacity before that protected period could run. Otherwise United could grow using its additional gates while American waited for its own, and then the city would use the unequal flying to take gates away from American. The way gates work at Chicago O’Hare is that prior flying determines future gate space (or, technically, ‘linear frontage’).

That’s the problem I identified when American first filed its lawsuit. The timing was part of the bargain that got American to support the redevelopment agreement in the first place.

And the trial judget accepted that the city and American had agreed to tie the process to the three additional gates becoming operational:

For purposes of this motion, that much—the Court has no doubt—was the deal.

His position, though, is that the city’s fingers were crossed, suggesting that the explicit written commitment didn’t make it into the final lease, or at least that American couldn’t establish that it had:

American’s last additional gate became operational March 14, 2025. Under its reading, the protected year therefore ran through March 2026, and the next redetermination could begin April 1, 2027. Chicago instead treated the protected period as having begun in December 2023, allowing redistribution in 2025.

The city’s reading is silly. The map is part of the signed agreement. Requiring the city to deliver the capacity shown there before starting a year of protected assignments doesn’t require inventing a promise outside the contract. And designating a gate common use doesn’t explain how a gate that isn’t operational can fulfill a promise intended to let an airline ramp up flying.

The appellate court assumed American could satisfy the initial requirements for an injunction and still concluded that the harm from blocking the gate changes justified denying one. It was reviewing whether the trial judge abused his discretion, NOT deciding the contract dispute from scratch. American’s problem was that it didn’t establish losing the gates would destroy its Chicago hub. It planned to operate the same number of flights using fewer gates, with more flying at less attractive times and less room to recover from delays. That could cost money, make operations worse and harm passengers but it made the injury look measurable. That was my original point – that this would be a case for future damages rather than an injunction. Meanwhile, the other airlines had planned schedules around the redistribution. United projected more than 2,000 cancellations if it were blocked. That number was overblown but the court accepted that changing the arrangements would disrupt passengers, other airlines, and airport construction. And the expectation that American would win gates back in the next allocation (which it did) undercut the argument that it faced an irreversible decline. Timing hurt American, too. Chicago announced the redistribution in February 2025. American sued in May but didn’t request preliminary relief until July. By the September hearing, the October gate changes were imminent and preparations were well underway. American argued that the city shouldn’t get to invoke the hardships from correcting an agreement they deliberately broke. The appeals court rejected that approach because it saw a reasonable dispute over what the contract meant. In my view, Chicago (intentionally) muddied the contract issue enough to make it less clear. This decision doesn’t end American’s lawsuit. It upholds the denial of a preliminary injunction. The contract claims and potential damages are still unresolved. The court rejected the argument that implementation of the gate changes had made the appeal moot, since a court could still order an effective remedy. United’s strategy ran into the airport’s actual capacity Chicago seemed strongly inclined to help its hometown airline. United’s headquarters are valuable to the city, especially with rumors of a move to Denver hanging over the relationship. My coverage of the gate dispute even generated an angry phone call from Chicago “shadow mayor” Jason Lee. United saw a chance to turn American’s slow recovery from the pandemic into a permanent retreat. American had retired too many aircraft and couldn’t rebuild everywhere at once. Fewer Chicago departures meant fewer gates, which could make future growth harder. United CEO Scott Kirby tried to create pressure by talking up American’s Chicago losses and getting financial analysts to question why it should stay. United then announced additional flying on the morning of American’s earnings call, practically writing the questions for them. This was strategic flying. United clearly didn’t want all of that additional capacity. It wanted invesors to believe that any growth would be matched, so American couldn’t improve its gate position and would just lose more money trying. Kirby told analysts United would add “as many flights as are required” to protect its gate count. Then the Federal Aviation Administration intervened. The airport couldn’t handle the schedules airlines were filing, especially with construction constraining movement on the ground. Its summer order capped scheduled arrivals and departures at 2,708 per day from May 17 through October 24. The government used approved summer 2025 schedules as its baseline. It rejected rewarding airlines for filing unrealistic 2026 schedules to improve their negotiating position. United’s much larger proposed buildup didn’t entitle it to preserve that bigger share while forcing American to shrink. The government effectively called United’s bluff. The cap limited American, too, but it protected the existing competitive balance against United’s attempt to overwhelm it with additional flights. American had also grown enough during 2025 to earn back gate space in October’s redistribution. The returned space amounts to roughly three narrowbody gate equivalents. Separately, American acquired Spirit’s G8 and G10 gate leases for $30 million, which I was first to report. That reduces the practical stakes of this appeal, but it still seems that Chicago broke its agreement to benefit United. you almost think DL decided to get out of the central terminal and into terminal 5 not just to avoid the costs of the rebuild but also to set up this catfight between AA and UA.

It is also certain that AA failed to look down the road to realize it needed to protect its ORD gates – many of which it did not use because the aircraft were repositioned to its failed AUS experiment. But the judge is correct that the City of Chicago made enough promises and put them in writing that AA does have the basis for the case to keep going.

UA has failed at not only pushing AA out of ORD – AA’s revenue rehab efforts are going well enough that they can afford to selectively invest in what strategically matters – but also in preventing UA from building a megahub that it dominates as DL does at ATL and AA does at DFW and to a lesser extent CLT. The competitive environment at ORD is obvious from average fares that are $100 lower than DL gets at MSP and DTW and over $50 less than AA gets at DFW and DL gets at ATL. ORD is just a financial drag for both AA and UA.

this could have turned out much worse for AA but they have what they need to fight at ORD.

During my time living in the Chicago area from the 1980s through the late 2010s, I first started flying mostly with American. They were the first airline where I got a free family trip, mostly thanks to matching a promotion Midway Airlines ran. I was never a frequent enough traveler to keep my miles active, and they would frequently expire. In my later years in Chicago, I flew more on United, as it had better international options than American. AA didn’t fly to Paris, it’s flights to Tel Aviv were not as convenient, and their Asian options were limited. This put nearly all of my flying on United. I was almost never more than Silver, as all my flying was in the cheap seats.

To capture more passengers, AA needs more international flights from Chicago to both Europe and Asia, and they need more airplanes, and likely the new international terminal to provide more international gates. The international flights could bring them more relevance for both local travelers and connecting travelers to those flights. And this will cause those travelers to take more AA domestic flights, where the bread and butter of revenue comes from, as well as drive more revenue.

I don’t understand why Kirby uses a competing airline’s profitability as a rationale for trying to force them out of a market. He made similar comments when DL initiated, or reinitiated their HKG route.

Remaining in an unprofitable market is the airline’s and their Board’s decision.

Kirby loves press coverage but his ongoing rants only further hinders his credibility.

Perhaps his time would be better invested in improving his customers’ experience at the service level. An extensive route network is only one component of an airline’s reputation.

#5963. Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees

The ‘blue slip’ privilege lets a single senator thwart a power that constitutionally belongs to the president and the entire Senate.

Senator John Cornyn (R., Texas) attends a hearing on nominations for director of national intelligence on Capitol Hill, November 18, 2026.

Senator John Cornyn recently blocked the nomination of the eminently qualified T. Elliot Gaiser to the federal district court in Texas, preferring a favorite-son candidate whom President Trump did not nominate. But the Constitution is clear: The nomination belongs to the president, not the distinguished senator. The constitutional power to “advise and consent” does not belong to a single senator, but to the Senate as a whole. Senator Cornyn’s use of a long-standing privilege conveyed by his colleagues usurps the power of both the president and the Senate.

The “blue slip” privilege does not exist in the Constitution or even in the Senate Rules. It is a practice of the Judiciary Committee not to advance a judicial nominee to a vote without the approval of both of the State’s senators. Invented in 1916, its scope and application are entirely within the discretion of the Senate Judiciary chairman, Chuck Grassley. He ought to use his discretion to put Gaiser’s nomination to a vote.

Dave Yost is senior counsel and vice president of policy innovation at Alliance Defending Freedom. He previously served as the attorney general of Ohio.

On “Lame-Duck Senators Should Not Be Able to Block Good Judicial Nominees”

#5962. American Airlines Passenger Admits Taking Business Class Pillows—The Airline Calls It A Favorite Confession

An American Airlines passenger confessed to taking home two pillows from international business class. Their husband sleeps with one every night and can’t sleep without it. The second pillow is a backup. American told them it was delighted the pillows had found a loving home. That’s a very different reaction from United Airlines, which told flight attendants to stop passengers from taking its Polaris bedding. And I think American has the right instinct here. A passenger is still talking about how much they love the airline’s business class product a year after the flight. This is also an unusually good advertisement for an airline pillow. We have to admit… this may be one of our favorite confessions. We’re glad those pillows found such a loving home, and even happier to hear they’re still helping you both get a great night’s sleep! Thank you for sharing the laugh and for choosing to fly with us. — americanair (@AmericanAir) November 20, 2026 I Have Airline Blankets On My Couch On my couch at home I have American Airlines blankets from before the US Airways merger, along with Etihad first class blankets. The Etihad ones are some of the softest, most comfortable blankets I’ve ever used. They remind me of those flights, and make me want to get back on board. About a year ago, at American’s event introducing its Airbus A321XLR, I took home a 100th anniversary pillow. (With permission.) When my daughter was in preschool, parents sent their kids with sleep sacks for nap time. I sent her with a United Polaris cooling gel pillow. United actually sent me a cooling gel pillow in a promotional package in 2018. They understood the value of getting the product into someone’s home when it was their public relations team doing the sending. So it was even more odd to see passengers spending thousands of dollars with them as scoflaws. An airline can buy advertising to tell me its business class bed is comfortable. A blanket I actually use at home lets me experience a little of that comfort again. An unusual souvenir also gives someone a reason to ask about a trip. Now I’m telling the story of the flight, remembering what I liked about it, and introducing somebody else to the product. United Wanted Its Pillows Back. Holiday Inn Gave Away More Towels. In 2017, United told flight attendants to watch for passengers taking its new Saks Fifth Avenue bedding. all pillows and blankets are to be left on the aircraft at the end of each flight, including the cooling gel memory foam pillow. United said even a few missing items per flight could add up to millions of dollars across its network. They laundered and reused the bedding over multiple flights. The same instructions allowed passengers to take amenity kits, slippers and pajamas where offered. I argued that United should see the marketing opportunity. They’d finally developed bedding that customers actively wanted to bring home! There ought to be a way to take advantage of that enthusiasm. Holiday Inn did. Back in 2003, I wrote about its towel amnesty. The IHG brand declared August 28 Towel Amnesty Day and forgave guests who’d taken towels over the years. They didn’t just promise not to chase anyone. Their original announcement included more than 60,000 souvenir towels to give away, plus a dollar for Give Kids The World for every towel story collected. They turned missing inventory into stories about people’s stays. In 2013, Hyatt actively encouraged guests to take its bath amenities. Those little bottles could remind you of the hotel the next time you used them. That meant the toiletries supplied in your room, not clearing out a housekeeping cart. And it doesn’t translate into permission to remove today’s large communal shampoo dispensers. What a shame those germ farms are. Some Of The Best Airline Souvenirs Are Meant To Leave Airlines already know that small objects can become a reason to remember them, talk about them, and even book them again. KLM’s Delft houses. The airline gives miniature Dutch buildings filled with Dutch gin to intercontinental business class passengers. They’ve been doing it since the 1950s, and release a new house each year on their October 7 anniversary. There’s even an app to track your collection. The airline has given you something to collect on a future trip. Lufthansa’s rubber ducks. These began in the bathrooms of the Frankfurt First Class Terminal in 2004. Lufthansa’s own anniversary history describes delighted guests taking them home. The airline embraced it and created special editions. A little bath toy became a recognizable part of an expensive first class experience. Delta’s trading cards. You can ask a pilot for one. Delta says it distributed more than 3 million in 2024 and produced over 5 million for its 2025 collection. This works in coach, too. The souvenir comes with a conversation with a pilot. Other airlines offer these now, too. Virgin Atlantic’s salt and pepper shakers. The little aircraft-shaped shakers famously carry the words “pinched from” and “Virgin Atlantic” underneath. The airline has joked publicly about passengers taking them. They’ve made the souvenir story part of the design, although I’d still ask before pocketing tableware. Virgin Australia had a particularly good version of this: its business class salt and pepper shakers fit together to make the Sydney Opera House. Passengers took them home. A generic salt shaker doesn’t give you much to talk about. A tiny Opera House does. Amenity Kits Are A Marketing Deal, Too An amenity kit is supposed to go home with you. The toothbrush and eye mask help during the flight. A useful bag can stay in your life for years. I’ve written about the economics of these partnerships, including United’s Brooks Brothers kits. The brand supplying the toiletries or putting its name on the bag can be subsidizing the airline’s cost. That may mean free or discounted products, shared costs, or payments for exposure to premium passengers. In other arrangements the airline pays for a luxury name. The skincare company gets its product into the hands of someone who might buy it again. The airline gets a more desirable amenity and an association with the brand. Taking the samples home and finishing them is part of the point. Where I’d Draw The Line For passengers, the starting point is what you’re being given. Amenity kits and their contents, pajamas and personal slippers where offered, children’s activity kits, and souvenirs handed out by the airline are generally yours to keep. Bedding, mattress pads, reusable noise cancelling headphones, glasses, dishes and metal cutlery are generally equipment for use during the flight. Ask before taking them. For the airline, I’d be generous with a small, distinctive item that a passenger loves, provided it’s inexpensive enough to give away and there’s enough stock to keep delivering the promised product. Give employees room to say yes. There are clear limits. Hotel guests taking televisions is absurd. I’ve covered hotels reporting stolen mattresses. That’s a very different reaction from United Airlines, which told flight attendants to stop passengers from taking its Polaris bedding. And I think American has the right instinct here. Lufthansa’s own anniversary history describes delighted guests taking them home. The airline embraced it and created special editions. A little bath toy became a recognizable part of an expensive first class experience. Delta’s trading cards. You can ask a pilot for one. Delta says it distributed more than 3 million in 2024 and produced over 5 million for its 2025 collection. This works in coach, too. The souvenir comes with a conversation with a pilot. Other airlines offer these now, too. Virgin Atlantic’s salt and pepper shakers. The little aircraft-shaped shakers famously carry the words “pinched from” and “Virgin Atlantic” underneath. The airline has joked publicly about passengers taking them. They’ve made the souvenir story part of the design, although I’d still ask before pocketing tableware. Gary Leff is one of the foremost experts in the field of miles, points, and frequent business travel - a topic he has covered since 2002. Co-founder of frequent flyer community InsideFlyer.com, emcee of the Freddie Awards, and named one of the "World's Top Travel Experts" by Conde' Nast Traveler (2010-Present) Gary has been a guest on most major news media, profiled in several top print publications, and published broadly on the topic of consumer loyalty. More About Gary »

Pan Am would hand out small carry bags to celebrities with the corporate logo. Back then, Hollywood stars would have their picture taken as they walked down the mobile stairs to the tarmac while arriving in Paris, London, or Rome to shoot a movie. Also, the airlines would have its name or logo just inside the exit door of the prop or jet for additional photo publicity. If in doubt, just Google photos of when the Beetles arrive at JFK in 1964; John Lennon has a Pan Am bag in his hand.

I have the blue thin Delta blankets ( turned them into rags ), red AA thin blankets ( my dogs sleep on them ), and the newish thicker UA blankets ( from my recent trip to HKG ). Up next: Cathay blankets on my Feb trip.

I still have one of those PanAm bags given to me when I bought a ticket in F to Tokyo at their NYC office back in the 70’s. That flight was on their 747SP nonstop.

What kind of low life rips off bedding from their flight.

Bunch of thieves on these planes. Explains a lot when you think about it…

Gotta love people who rationalize stealing.

Weird to take a biz class pillow, but if you really think that will change your life, I say go for it. AA is wise to play along. Better to get the brand endorsement than look like a cheap scold.

I have some really soft warm blankets from American international first class that were brought home years ago along with wine glasses from BA Concorde, Easterna and Pan Am first class and I treasure these wonderful souvenirs and wonderful memories.

When you pay $10K+ for a roundtrip to Europe, cash, then does it really matter?

Sure, the points people and hoarders are gonna hoard, but surely, it doesn’t even register a rounding error against $10K for 7 hours of flight time.

When UA first rolled out its Polaris bedding, I commented to an FA what a great travel pillow they had. The FA told me to take it if I wanted. I still use it a lot, and there is the association with UA as the cover is emblazoned with “United” and “Polaris”–a constant reminder and, to me, great marketing. Same with the pajamas. But they’ve cut back on everything, which I think is a mistake, especially with other airlines stepping up.

As TPG's cruise team lead, Gene Sloan oversees the site's cruise content and also writes many of TPG's main cruise guides. He has spent nearly 30 years writing about cruise ships and cruising, and he is one of the world's best-known authorities on the topic.

Belinda Luksic is an Australian travel journalist with words published across the globe, including in Conde Nast Traveler, Travel + Leisure Asia and Robb Report. Her work has taken her to all seven continents and both poles, where she has swum with whale sharks in Ningaloo Reef, plunged into the icy waters of the North Pole, eaten crickets in Siem Reap, hiked ancient trails in Bhutan and cycled the Balkans solo. She is an expert on Croatia and Hungary, and specializes in small ship and expedition cruising, luxury, food, wine and soft adventure. Sydney-born, she now divides her time between Australia, Croatia (where she holds dual citizenship) and the United States.

There is no shortage of choices for a cruise to the Caribbean — the most popular cruise destination in the world. More than 200 cruise ships spend at least part of every year in the region, and cruise-selling websites list thousands of individual Caribbean sailings.

This can be great news for would-be Caribbean cruisers, but it can also be overwhelming. With so many options, where do you even begin? Which one of these ships and sailings is the best?

We get the latter question a lot, and we always answer the same noncommittal way: It depends. The best ship and sailing in the Caribbean for whom? The best for us? The best for you? The best for your kids?

When picking the best cruise in the Caribbean, as with choosing the best cruise anywhere, a lot comes down to personal tastes and preferences. Some people love the big-resort feel of the biggest-of-big ships. Others are horrified by the very idea of them. Some people demand (and are willing to pay for) the highest levels of luxury. Others are on tight budgets. The best cruise for a family with kids isn’t necessarily the same as the best cruise for a couple looking for romance.

What kind of cruiser are you? It’s important to think that through before narrowing down your choices.

The bottom line is that the best Caribbean cruise for you depends a lot on your travel style. Below, we'll help you narrow your choices by looking at Caribbean cruises by category. The good news is that in the Caribbean, there really is something for everyone.

If your idea of a great vacation is a week at a big, bustling resort filled with every sort of amusement known to humans, you'll probably want to start your Caribbean cruise search with a look at the biggest vessels from lines like Royal Caribbean.

If "more is better" is your mantra, skip the search and look up Legend of the Seas, the newest of the Icon class ships.

At nearly 250,000 gross tons, the 20-deck-high vessel is among the world’s biggest cruise ships, alongside its sister ships Icon of the Seas and Star of the Seas.

Some of the wow factors on these Icon Class ships include massive water parks, cantilevered infinity pools, huge glass domes encompassing an indoor AquaTheater for acrobatic and diving shows, and innovative new cabin and suite layouts for families.

Legend of the Seas will depart Fort Lauderdale, Florida, on six-, seven-, and eight-night Western and Southern Caribbean itineraries.

Southern Caribbean sailings head to the ABC islands and stop at Perfect Day at CocoCay. Prices at about $1,509 per person, based on double occupancy.

Western Caribbean itineraries call at Costa Maya and Cozumel in Mexico as well as at Perfect Day at CocoCay. Prices start at $1,264 per person, based on double occupancy.

With at least two sea days per sailing, passengers will have ample opportunity to explore all the attractions the ship has to offer.

Related: Yikes, does Royal Caribbean’s new Icon of the Seas really cost that much?

In the family cruise arena, it’s hard to top Disney Cruise Line. As you might expect, the line caters heavily to families in every way, from onboard attractions to family-friendly cabin configurations.

Disney's special brand of magic translates just as well at sea. Kids receive the royal treatment with high-quality kids’ clubs and onboard attractions such as the 765-foot-long AquaMouse water coaster. Plus, there are plenty of chances for photo ops with their favorite Disney characters.

Parents will find opportunities to unwind at adults-only sundecks and pool areas that are closed to kids; there are also bars and clubs that are off-limits to anyone younger than 18.

Additionally, many cabins on Disney ships feature extra pull-down bunks and sofa beds, allowing four or even five people to stay in a single cabin. Most cabins have two bathrooms — one with a sink and a toilet, and the other with a sink and a shower or tub. This is rare in the cruise world, and it's designed to make it easier for families sharing a room to get ready.

For family fun on the high seas, try a seven-night Eastern Caribbean cruise aboard Disney Treasure. Departing from Port Canaveral, the ship stops in Tortola, British Virgin Islands; San Juan, Puerto Rico; and Castaway Cay, Disney's private island.

Sail on a themed cruise for Halloween or Christmas, and you can enjoy special onboard activities and events.

Prices for seven-night Caribbean sailings start at $3,648 for two people sharing a cabin.

Related: The ultimate guide to Disney Cruise Line ships and itineraries

When it comes to affordability, the undisputed leader in the Caribbean cruise market is Carnival Cruise Line. Not only does Carnival offer lower fares than you'll find at most rival lines, but it also purposely deploys its Caribbean-focused vessels to a wider variety of U.S. home ports than any other line. The idea is that a large percentage of the U.S. population can reach a Caribbean-bound Carnival ship by car, saving the cost of flights.

Related: The ultimate guide to Carnival Cruise Line ships and itineraries

Carnival ships are packed with fun-focused attractions, including multiple pool areas, water parks with waterslides, basketball courts, miniature golf courses and even roller coasters on select ships.

The cruise line is known for its multitude of included-in-the-fare dining spots. Every vessel has two main dining rooms and a casual buffet eatery. Most ships feature two of the best quick-serve poolside dining venues you'll find on mass-market ships at sea: BlueIguana Cantina for burritos and tacos, and Guy's Burger Joint.

Carnival ships sail to the Caribbean from all the major Florida cruise hubs but also from ports as far-flung as Baltimore; Norfolk, Virginia; Mobile, Alabama; New Orleans; and Galveston, Texas.

The line's seven-day Western Caribbean sailings from New Orleans on Carnival Liberty are a solid choice for budget-minded travelers seeking an affordable Caribbean escape from the middle part of America. Stops include the Honduran island of Roatan; Belize City, Belize; and Cozumel.

Rates for seven-day sailings out of New Orleans start at $444 per person, based on double occupancy.

Related: 6 ways to get a deal on a cruise

Looking to dip your toes into cruising for the first time, but not sure you'll love it? A great option in the Bahamas and Caribbean region is Margaritaville at Sea.

Founded in 2022, the Florida-based brand is particularly known for short and affordable sailings that offer the perfect entry to cruising for someone who isn't yet ready to commit to something longer and more expensive.

The line's original vessel, Margaritaville at Sea Paradise, operates out of West Palm Beach, Florida, with sailings as short as two days — an unusually short length in a market where most sailings are at least three nights or longer. These short two-night sailings start at just $189 per person, based on double occupancy.

At that length and price, even if you discover cruising isn't for you, you haven't committed all that much in time and money to figuring that out.

But you may very well find that you love it — particularly the sort of cruising that Margaritaville at Sea offers.

With its ships themed around the signature laid-back, Jimmy Buffett–inspired aesthetic that Parrotheads have come to love, the brand leans into a fun, social atmosphere (as the song says, "It's five o'clock somewhere"). It's more laid-back than the traditional party-focused vibe you find on some lines.

And should you eventually want to try a longer cruise, Margaritaville at Sea now offers those, too. In addition to two-night sailings, Margaritaville at Sea Paradise also operates three-, four- and five-night voyages out of West Palm Beach. The addition of a second ship in 2024 — the Tampa-based Margaritaville at Sea Islander — brought sailings as long as 10 nights.

Rates for four-night sailings out of West Palm Beach start at $149 per person, based on double occupancy.

When it comes to solo cruisers, the king of the hill in the Caribbean is Norwegian Cruise Line — at least, among the big-ship lines. In 2010, the Miami-based cruise operator began adding entire zones for solo travelers to the center of every new ship it deployed to the region.

You’ll now find these zones on Caribbean-focused vessels like Norwegian Encore, Norwegian Breakaway, Norwegian Getaway, Norwegian Epic and Norwegian Prima. Each of these solo cruiser zones, which are unrepeated in the industry for now, includes dozens of cabins for solo travelers, all clustered together. There is also a private lounge with a bar and a TV where solos can mingle at daily happy-hour gatherings.

Known as Studio cabins, the tiny solo rooms in these complexes measure just 100 square feet, but they're superbly designed to maximize storage space. The cabins' futuristic design and the multicolored mood lighting are particularly noteworthy.

Related: These 8 solo cruise cabins are great for travelers sailing alone

One big caveat about Norwegian's solo cabins: Most are interior rooms without an ocean view. Instead, they have windows overlooking a corridor. Another downside is that these cabins are so popular that they often sell out far in advance, sometimes at fares not much lower than fares for a cabin booked for two.

Single cruisers seeking rest and relaxation should consider the seven-night Caribbean sailings aboard Norwegian Luna, which depart from Miami.

The 3,550-passenger ship offers no shortage of restaurants, bars, late-night entertainment, comedy and slick theater shows, including the tribute show, "Elton: A Celebration of Elton John." Norwegian's freestyle dining is another boon for solo travelers. Rather than being locked into set dining times with strangers, passengers are free to dine with newfound friends at a time that suits them.

Norwegian Luna sails the eastern and western Caribbean on seven-night sailings out of Miami. Western Caribbean cruises also include a day at Great Stirrup Cay, Norwegian's private island in the Bahamas, which is home to the Caribbean's largest water park.

Rates for a Studio cabin start at $398 per person.

Related: The best credit cards for booking cruises

For those who wouldn’t be caught dead on a vessel that doesn’t have butler service and free-flowing caviar, the Caribbean can be a tough spot. Many of the world’s most luxurious cruise ships spend a lot of time in Europe and Asia or on round-the-world cruises. For some luxury lines, the Caribbean is almost an afterthought.

Luxury sailings in the Caribbean are also concentrated in the winter months, from December through March. Between April and October, options are much more limited.

However, if an upscale cruise experience is what you seek, Seabourn Cruises can deliver. The line's seven-day "Caribbean Gems" itinerary aboard Seabourn Ovation should be on your radar.

Seabourn specializes in small ships carrying fewer than 600 passengers. The line markets its vessels as luxury ships with a yacht-like atmosphere, while still offering familiar cruise-ship amenities, including indoor lounges and multiple restaurants and bars.

The 600-passenger Seabourn Ovation offers all-suite accommodations, with every suite featuring a private verandah. These range in size from 251-square-foot entry-level suites to the 1,306-square-foot owner’s suites.

Along with a lavish spa and fitness center, multiple pools, restaurants and bars, and a dedicated sushi bar, Seabourn Ovation offers butler service and the line's signature caviar service, available anytime, anywhere.

Rates start at $3,279 per person, based on double occupancy.

Virgin Voyages appeals to vacationers averse to the traditional cruising experience who crave a hip, party atmosphere. Ships are blissfully free of children — cruisers must be over 18 — making it a prime choice for an adults-only cruise.

Virgin has unique onboard offerings such as the first tattoo parlor at sea, numerous included dining options, free exercise classes and an app that lets you simply shake your phone to order Champagne (which can then be delivered just about anywhere on board). Fares also include all meals, soda and basic Wi-Fi.

Virgin's first vessel, Scarlet Lady, launched in late 2021, and the line has since added three more ships: Valiant Lady, Resilient Lady and Brilliant Lady.

Ships are filled with stylish, adult-oriented bars promising a hopping scene late into the night, as well as hipster venues like a colorful karaoke lounge. Onboard entertainment is inventive and often edgier than what you might see on traditional cruises.

Cabins sport a minimalist look with futuristic touches, and suites exude a rock 'n' roll vibe with in-room turntables and peekaboo showers.

The line's five-night "Dominican Republic and Bimini Beach Club" itinerary — which visits Bimini, Bahamas, and Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic — is available on multiple ships out of Miami and is a top option. With two sea days, the sailing offers a good mix of onboard activities and port-of-call exploration. Party by the pool or swim with stingrays during your day at Virgin Voyages' Bimini Beach Club. Chill out on a powder-white beach or go waterfall hunting in the jungle in the Dominican Republic.

Rates start at $695 per person, based on double occupancy.

Related: Virgin Voyages cruise cabins and suites: Everything you want to know

For couples wanting to dial up the romance, Windstar Cruises offers a more intimate way to explore the Caribbean. Its small, yacht-like ships cruise at a leisurely pace, anchoring off small islands and calling at quiet harbors far from the big-ship crowds.

Windstar specializes in small ships carrying between 148 and 342 passengers each. The line calls them yachts, but the ships are more like small cruise ships, with indoor lounges and communal dining rooms.

The line's seven-night "Classic Caribbean" itinerary aboard Wind Surf is a good choice for couples, with stops at some of the region's most appealing islands.

The five-masted vessel carries just 342 passengers and offers four types of accommodations, ranging in size from 188-square-foot cabins to 376-square-foot suites.

None has a private balcony, but the ship's open decks offer plenty of room to take in the views.

One of Windstar's biggest draws is its watersports platform, which opens at the stern when the ship is anchored and conditions permit. Couples can go kayaking or stand-up paddleboarding, swim in the sea or simply float in the water while taking in the views of a harbor dotted with yachts.

Back on board, Wind Surf has multiple dining venues, a pool, hot tubs, a spa and a fitness center. The ship's smaller scale also makes for a less crowded experience than you'll find on the big resort-style ships.

The seven-night "Classic Caribbean" itinerary begins and ends in St. Maarten. Expect sun-kissed beaches, secret coves and gin-clear waters in idyllic ports like St. Barts, St. Kitts and Nevis, Guadeloupe, Dominica and St. Lucia.

All-inclusive rates start at $2,922 per person and cover Wi-Fi, gratuities and unlimited beer, wine and cocktails.

#5960. Tempers flare as future of Social Security debated

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday showed how poisonous the politics could become.

Budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

“I think it’s outrageous,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”

Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

"This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”

But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”

In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”

Johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a plan in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

Senators on both sides of the aisle said they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

“I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability issue, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.
